rows.name: The Linux Command Line (free online book)
rows.summary: Beginner-friendly book that walks through the shell, files, processes and scripting.
rows.accessNote: Free to read online under CC BY-NC-ND; a printed edition is optional and not required.
outcomes: Move around a filesystem and control permissions from the shell
Manage processes, packages and users
Write a shell script that does something you needed
rows.assumes: Nothing — it starts at the prompt.
rows.limits: Command-line skills only: no kernel internals, no service architecture, and no substitute for administering a real machine.
rows.commitment: Weeks at an hour a day.

rows.name: MDN Web Docs
rows.summary: Reference documentation for HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with accessibility guidance.
rows.accessNote: Free and openly licensed (CC BY-SA for most content).
outcomes: Look up any HTML, CSS or JavaScript feature and its browser support
Check your own markup against the accessibility guidance
Follow the Learn path from first page to a working site
rows.assumes: Nothing for the reference; basic familiarity for the tutorials.
rows.limits: A reference first and a tutorial second — it will not take you from nothing to deployed on its own.
rows.commitment: Reference: use as needed. The Learn path: weeks.

rows.name: Mechanics Map
rows.summary: Open textbook for statics and dynamics, with worked examples, free-body diagrams and interactive activities.
rows.accessNote: Free to read online under an open licence, no account required. Some activities are PDF downloads that also work offline.
outcomes: Resolve forces and find reactions on beams, trusses and frames
Locate a centroid and compute a section’s moment of inertia
Analyse friction and equilibrium for a real component, not a diagram
rows.assumes: Algebra and trigonometry; calculus only in the later dynamics chapters.
rows.limits: Mechanics only: it stops before strength of materials, so stress, deflection and safety factors are elsewhere.
rows.commitment: A semester-scale textbook; chapters stand alone as references.

rows.name: MIT 2.810: Manufacturing Processes and Systems (course site)
rows.summary: Lecture material on process physics and manufacturing systems, with a hands-on group fabrication project.
rows.accessNote: The course site with lecture material, schedule and project description is free to read. It is not an enrolment and carries no credit.
outcomes: Understand how process physics and randomness set quality, rate and cost
Connect a manufacturing process to the part design it implies
See how a fabrication project is scoped and assessed at university level
rows.assumes: Materials science and mechanics at undergraduate level.
rows.limits: A course site rather than a packaged course: no videos, no forum, and the laboratory and machine shop are obviously unavailable remotely.
rows.commitment: A semester if worked against the schedule.

rows.name: MIT OCW 16.01: Unified Engineering
rows.summary: Integrated aerospace fundamentals: materials, structures, fluids and thermodynamics.
rows.accessNote: Free under CC BY-NC-SA.
outcomes: Work across structures, fluids, materials and thermodynamics in one frame
Analyse aerospace components conceptually before reaching for software
Read the field’s standard references with context
rows.assumes: Physics, calculus and statics; this is a demanding course.
rows.limits: MIT’s term structure with heavy problem sets, and no flight-test or hands-on laboratory component.
rows.commitment: A full term, if not a year.

rows.name: MIT OpenCourseWare: Materials for Biomedical Applications (3.051J)
rows.summary: Materials science applied to the body: structure, properties, degradation and host response.
rows.accessNote: Lecture notes, assignments and exams are free under a Creative Commons licence; no video for this edition.
outcomes: Relate material structure and processing to what happens when it is implanted
Reason about degradation, corrosion and wear in a physiological environment
Assess a material choice against a specific application and its service life
rows.assumes: Materials science, chemistry and some thermodynamics.
rows.limits: No laboratory work is included, and regulatory testing standards are not covered.
rows.commitment: A semester course.

rows.name: MIT OpenCourseWare: Biomedical Signal and Image Processing (HST.582J)
rows.summary: Course on processing biomedical signals and images: filtering, detection, estimation and imaging reconstruction.
rows.provider: MIT OpenCourseWare (Harvard-MIT Health Sciences and Technology)
rows.accessNote: Lecture notes, problem sets, labs and some exams are free under a Creative Commons licence; no certificate and no grading.
outcomes: Apply filtering, detection and estimation to ECG and other physiological signals
Understand how projection data becomes a CT image
Work through a laboratory exercise on real biomedical data
rows.assumes: Signals and systems, probability and linear algebra at undergraduate level.
rows.limits: No video lectures for this edition, and the labs expect data you must supply yourself.
rows.commitment: A graduate-level semester.

rows.name: MIT OCW 6.002: Circuits and Electronics
rows.summary: University circuits course taught from first principles, with the full lecture videos and problem sets.
rows.accessNote: Free under CC BY-NC-SA, including the lecture videos and assignments. No account and no payment.
outcomes: Analyse circuits with node and mesh methods instead of guessing
Reason about amplifiers, small-signal models and feedback
Understand why digital abstraction works on top of analogue physics
rows.assumes: Calculus and differential equations taken or in progress.
rows.limits: Theory at MIT pace with no laboratory: measurement, breadboarding and simulation practice come from elsewhere.
rows.commitment: A semester of lectures.

rows.name: MIT OCW 2.007: Design and Manufacturing I
rows.summary: Design-and-build course where students machine parts to tolerance and assemble a working machine.
rows.accessNote: Free under CC BY-NC-SA. The course had a shop and a competition: lectures, notes and assignments are online, the machines are not.
outcomes: Design a part so that it can actually be machined and assembled
Read a drawing with tolerances and datums on it
Choose a process — milling, turning, sheet, printing — for a given feature
rows.assumes: Basic mechanics and a willingness to think in three dimensions.
rows.limits: Shop practice cannot be learned from a video: the hands-on half needs machines and supervision. Process selection is covered; detailed tooling data is not.
rows.commitment: A semester course; the design lectures also work as a standalone read.

rows.name: MIT OCW 18.03: Differential Equations
rows.summary: Differential equations with engineering applications and simulations.
rows.accessNote: Free under CC BY-NC-SA.
outcomes: Solve first- and second-order equations and linear systems
Use Laplace transforms and matrix methods where they are quicker
Model oscillations, circuits and mixing problems end to end
rows.assumes: Single-variable calculus; linear algebra helps for the matrix chapters.
rows.limits: No partial differential equations and no numerical methods. The recordings come from one specific term, so the pacing is fixed.
rows.commitment: A semester of lectures.

rows.name: MIT OCW 18.06: Linear Algebra
rows.summary: Full MIT lecture series on matrices, vector spaces and eigenvalues.
rows.accessNote: Free under a CC BY-NC-SA licence. No certificate and no enrolment needed.
outcomes: Solve linear systems and reason about vector spaces and bases
Compute determinants, eigenvalues and diagonalisations
Recognise a linear problem and set it up as matrices before reaching for code
rows.assumes: Algebra; the course builds the linear algebra from the start.
rows.limits: Lectures only. Problem sets from that term are posted without full solutions, so self-checking takes discipline.
rows.commitment: About 35 lectures — a semester pace.

rows.name: MIT OpenCourseWare: Introduction to Manufacturing Systems (2.854)
rows.summary: Course on manufacturing systems: process variation, quality, capacity and system design.
rows.accessNote: Notes and assignments are free under a Creative Commons licence; no video for this edition and no certificate.
outcomes: Model a manufacturing system rather than a single machine
Quantify how process variation propagates into quality and yield
Analyse capacity and flow decisions with numbers
rows.assumes: Probability and statistics, plus some production experience or equivalent coursework.
rows.limits: A graduate-level treatment with limited worked solutions; the simulations expect you to supply data.
rows.commitment: A semester course.

rows.name: MIT OCW 6.033: Computer System Engineering
rows.summary: Networking, naming, security and reliability in computer systems.
rows.accessNote: Free under CC BY-NC-SA.
outcomes: Explain layering, naming and reliability as engineering trade-offs
Reason about a system’s failure modes rather than its API
Use the classic papers as a reading list
rows.assumes: Operating systems and programming; this is an advanced systems course.
rows.limits: Conceptual and paper-based: not a packet-level or configuration tutorial, and the labs are optional rather than required.
rows.commitment: A semester of lectures; the papers are a reading list you can revisit.

rows.name: MIT OpenCourseWare: Introduction to Operations Management (15.761)
rows.summary: Operations fundamentals: process analysis, queues, quality, inventory and lean operations.
rows.accessNote: Notes and assignments free under a Creative Commons licence; no video lectures for this edition.
outcomes: Analyse a process for capacity, bottlenecks and flow time
Apply queueing and inventory reasoning to service and production settings
Understand lean operations as a measurement discipline
rows.assumes: Basic algebra and some statistics; the course builds the queueing models it needs.
rows.limits: Business-school framing: strong on system behaviour, light on process physics and equipment.
rows.commitment: A semester; the case exercises take an hour each.

rows.name: MIT OCW 6.334: Power Electronics
rows.summary: Switching converters: how buck, boost and isolated topologies convert and control power efficiently.
rows.accessNote: Free under CC BY-NC-SA. Assignments are posted; laboratory benches obviously are not.
outcomes: Analyse the steady state of a buck or boost converter
Explain switching loss, ripple and why efficiency is a thermal problem
Choose a topology and a control approach for a stated load
rows.assumes: Circuit analysis, differential equations and some control theory.
rows.limits: Board-level analysis and design, without magnetics detail or layout: thermal and EMC practice sits outside the course.
rows.commitment: A semester, at advanced undergraduate pace.

rows.name: MIT OCW 6.622: Power Electronics
rows.summary: Modern treatment of switching converters and their control, with the full lecture videos.
rows.accessNote: Free under CC BY-NC-SA, including the lecture videos and problem sets. No lab hardware or design software.
outcomes: Analyse converter topologies with switching and loss in view
Design a control loop for a switching supply
See where magnetics, layout and thermal limits decide the result
rows.assumes: Circuits, control systems and differential equations.
rows.limits: Analysis and control rather than a full design flow: magnetics design and PCB layout are not covered.
rows.commitment: A semester. The 2007 course on this list covers the same ground more slowly.

rows.name: MIT OCW 6.061: Introduction to Electric Power Systems
rows.summary: University course on how AC power systems work, from three-phase quantities to stability.
rows.accessNote: Free under CC BY-NC-SA, lecture notes and assignments included. No laboratory or simulation licences.
outcomes: Explain why power flows the way it does on an AC network
Work with three-phase quantities and per-unit values
Reason about transformers, transmission limits and stability
rows.assumes: Circuit analysis, differential equations and complex numbers.
rows.limits: Theory and analysis at MIT pace: no protection engineering, no grid operations and no simulation tooling.
rows.commitment: A semester of lectures.

rows.name: MIT OpenCourseWare: Quantitative Physiology: Cells and Tissues (6.021J)
rows.summary: Physiology written as engineering: transport, membrane potentials and systems you can model.
rows.accessNote: Notes, assignments and exams are free under a Creative Commons licence; no solutions for every problem.
outcomes: Model transport, membrane potentials and cell signalling mathematically
Read physiology as a set of coupled differential equations rather than a list of facts
Build and analyse compartmental models of a physiological system
rows.assumes: Differential equations and some circuit theory for the membrane models.
rows.limits: Cells and tissues, not whole-body systems, and the edition is older than two decades.
rows.commitment: A semester of graduate-level study.

rows.name: MIT OpenCourseWare: Chemical and Biological Reaction Engineering (10.37)
rows.summary: Reaction rates, reactor design equations and multiple-reaction selectivity, including biological kinetics.
rows.accessNote: Lecture notes and problem sets free under a Creative Commons licence; no video lectures for this edition.
outcomes: Derive rate laws and reactor design equations from reaction mechanisms
Size batch, CSTR and plug-flow reactors for a stated duty
Analyse multiple reactions and selectivity, including enzyme and cell kinetics
rows.assumes: Material and energy balances, calculus and some physical chemistry.
rows.limits: No laboratory component and not every problem has a published solution: kinetics are handled on paper.
rows.commitment: A semester course.

rows.name: MIT OCW 2.12: Introduction to Robotics
rows.summary: Classic robotics course covering kinematics, actuators and sensing for manipulators.
rows.accessNote: Free under CC BY-NC-SA; lecture notes and assignments are posted without a lab kit, so the hardware exercises stay theoretical.
outcomes: Compute forward kinematics for a manipulator from its geometry
Use homogeneous transforms instead of ad-hoc trigonometry
Reason about actuators and sensing well enough to choose hardware
rows.assumes: Linear algebra and basic mechanics; programming helps for the assignments.
rows.limits: Older than the modern ROS-based courses: the mathematics is timeless, the tooling references are not, and there is no simulation.
rows.commitment: A semester course.

rows.name: MIT OpenCourseWare: Separation Processes (10.32)
rows.summary: Staged cascades and their application to distillation, absorption, adsorption and membranes.
rows.accessNote: Lecture notes, problem sets and exams are free under a Creative Commons licence; only some solutions are published.
outcomes: Design staged separations: distillation, absorption, adsorption and membranes
Use phase equilibria to establish the limit of what a separation can achieve
Estimate stage counts and reflux requirements for a stated purity
rows.assumes: Material and energy balances plus thermodynamics.
rows.limits: An older edition: conventions and property data date from 2005 and no simulation software is used.
rows.commitment: A semester; the problem sets are the substance of it.

rows.name: MIT OCW 6.003: Signals and Systems
rows.summary: How signals are represented, transformed and filtered: convolution, Fourier, Laplace and z-transforms.
rows.accessNote: Free under CC BY-NC-SA, with the full lecture videos and problem sets.
outcomes: Compute a convolution and explain why it is the operation that matters
Move between time and frequency domains with Fourier and Laplace
Design a simple filter and predict its response before measuring it
rows.assumes: Differential equations and complex numbers; linear algebra helps.
rows.limits: Continuous- and discrete-time theory with no implementation: no code, no hardware and no real sensor data.
rows.commitment: A semester of lectures.

rows.name: MIT OCW 3.032: Mechanical Behavior of Materials
rows.summary: Materials behaviour: elasticity, plasticity, fracture and fatigue.
rows.accessNote: Free under CC BY-NC-SA.
outcomes: Relate stress and strain through elastic and plastic regimes
Predict failure mechanisms: yielding, fracture, fatigue, creep
Choose a material with the failure mode in mind
rows.assumes: Statics and strength of materials.
rows.limits: Analytical treatment with no experimental laboratory component.
rows.commitment: A semester of lectures and problem sets.

rows.name: MIT OCW 18.05: Probability and Statistics
rows.summary: Probability, inference and Bayesian reasoning with engineering examples.
rows.accessNote: Free under CC BY-NC-SA.
outcomes: Work with probability distributions and expectations
Do hypothesis testing and interpret a p-value correctly
Update a belief with Bayesian reasoning
rows.assumes: Calculus; the course is mathematical rather than code-based.
rows.limits: Theory first: no data workflow and no software tutorial, so pair it with a practical resource.
rows.commitment: A semester of lectures and problem sets.

rows.name: MIT OCW 1.050: Solid Mechanics
rows.summary: Stress, strain, beam theory and structural analysis fundamentals.
rows.accessNote: Free under CC BY-NC-SA.
outcomes: Analyse beams, trusses and frames
Compute stress and deflection in typical members
Recognise when a structure is statically indeterminate and why it matters
rows.assumes: Statics and calculus.
rows.limits: Classical hand analysis: no finite-element software and no building-code compliance work.
rows.commitment: A semester of lectures and problem sets.

rows.name: MIT OpenCourseWare: Supply Chain Planning (15.762J)
rows.summary: Course on supply chain planning: forecasting, inventory, logistics and network design.
rows.accessNote: Notes, assignments and some exams free under a Creative Commons licence; no video lectures.
outcomes: Forecast demand and carry the uncertainty into inventory decisions
Design a distribution network and cost the alternatives
Recognise where lead-time variability changes the right answer
rows.assumes: Probability and statistics, plus basic optimisation.
rows.limits: An older edition with limited solutions and no software walk-through; spreadsheets are assumed.
rows.commitment: A semester course.

rows.name: MIT OpenCourseWare: Transport Processes (10.302)
rows.summary: University course on heat and mass transfer: conduction, diffusion, convection and radiation.
rows.accessNote: Notes, assignments and exams are free under a Creative Commons licence. This edition has no video lectures and no certificate.
outcomes: Derive conduction, convection and diffusion problems from first principles
Solve steady and transient heat and mass transfer problems of engineering significance
Read a transport problem and identify the mechanism that controls it
rows.assumes: Differential equations, fluid mechanics and thermodynamics at undergraduate level.
rows.limits: Assignments and exams come without published solutions, so you are your own marker and there is no forum.
rows.commitment: A full semester of study worked properly.

rows.name: Model Cards for Model Reporting
rows.summary: The paper that popularised documenting a model’s intended use and limitations.
rows.accessNote: Open-access preprint.
outcomes: Write a model card covering intended use, metrics and limits
Read someone else’s model card critically
Argue for disclosure of a model’s constraints
rows.assumes: Some machine-learning context; the paper is short and needs no deep maths.
rows.limits: One documentation framework, not a governance programme: it does not cover auditing, compliance or dataset licensing.
rows.commitment: An hour to read; a workshop to apply.

rows.name: Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control
rows.summary: The standard modern treatment of robot kinematics, dynamics, trajectory planning and control, with videos and software.
rows.accessNote: Free preprint chapters and lecture videos; the companion course can be audited free and the software library is open source.
outcomes: Compute forward and inverse kinematics for a manipulator
Represent configuration and motion without ambiguous Euler angles
Design a trajectory and a feedback controller for a simple arm
rows.assumes: Linear algebra, calculus and some programming; the book builds the rest.
rows.limits: Rigid-body manipulators in theory: no ROS integration, no perception, and little on prototyping or safety engineering.
rows.commitment: A graduate course: a term or two, or months of self-study.

rows.name: Microsoft Learn: Describe Cloud Computing
rows.summary: What cloud computing is: service and deployment models, shared responsibility, consumption pricing and elasticity.
rows.accessNote: Free with a Microsoft account; it prepares for a paid certification exam, but this module needs no payment or card.
outcomes: Explain IaaS, PaaS and SaaS by what you are responsible for
Distinguish public, private and hybrid deployment models
Read a cloud bill and see what actually drove the cost
rows.assumes: Nothing technical.
rows.limits: Microsoft-flavoured and certification-shaped: the concepts transfer, the service names do not, and it is not hands-on beyond quizzes.
rows.commitment: A few hours for this module; a week for the full fundamentals path.

rows.name: NASA Applied Remote Sensing Training (ARSET)
rows.summary: Free, agency-run trainings on remote sensing fundamentals and applications, with real data and certificates.
rows.accessNote: Free trainings with materials you keep; registration is free, and recorded sessions mean time zones rarely block you. Certificates of completion are issued for the assessed tracks.
outcomes: Learn remote sensing fundamentals from the agency that flies the instruments
Follow applied trainings on floods, land cover, air quality and more, with real data
Keep the materials and revisit the recordings
rows.assumes: None for the introductory tracks.
rows.limits: Course content is applied and agency-specific: exercises use NASA data and tools, and volunteer-run sessions vary in depth.
rows.commitment: Each training 4–12 h; a coherent track 30–60 h.

rows.name: NASA: Aerodynamics and Flight
rows.summary: Beginner-friendly explanations of lift, drag, thrust and flight controls.
rows.accessNote: US government material, generally free to use.
outcomes: Explain lift, drag, thrust and what control surfaces actually do
Read a lift curve or a flight envelope
Follow the aerodynamics of a real aircraft qualitatively
rows.assumes: School physics; algebra at most.
rows.limits: Explanatory pages rather than a course: little problem-solving practice, and parts are pitched at school level.
rows.commitment: An afternoon; revisit as needed.

rows.name: Neo4j Cypher Manual
rows.summary: Graph modelling and Cypher query language reference used by GraphMentor itself.
rows.accessNote: Documentation is free to read. A Neo4j AuraDB Free instance is free but has documented limits.
outcomes: Write Cypher matches, patterns and variable-length paths
Model a domain as nodes and relationships instead of tables
See why a graph query is shaped differently from a join
rows.assumes: Some SQL or data-modelling background helps considerably.
rows.limits: Cypher and modelling only: deployment, tuning and cost are elsewhere, and AuraDB Free has documented limits.
rows.commitment: Reference; the tutorials take an afternoon.

rows.name: NIST AI Risk Management Framework
rows.summary: Voluntary framework for managing the risks an AI system creates.
rows.accessNote: A US government publication, free to download and reuse. The companion playbook is free as well.
outcomes: Structure an AI risk discussion around the framework’s functions
Ask the questions a model’s documentation usually dodges
Tell governance work apart from engineering work
rows.assumes: Some machine-learning and organisational context.
rows.limits: Voluntary organisational guidance, not a technical course: it audits nothing and makes no model fairer by itself.
rows.commitment: Days to read; months to apply.

rows.name: NIST Cybersecurity Framework
rows.summary: Structured framework for organising security activities across an organisation.
rows.accessNote: US government publication, free to download and reuse.
outcomes: Describe the framework’s functions and how they map onto an organisation
Use it to structure a security conversation with non-specialists
Recognise that it is a risk-management structure, not a checklist
rows.assumes: Some organisational or security context; it is not a technical tutorial.
rows.limits: Voluntary, US-government framing: it does not tell you how to implement a control, and the references shift between revisions.
rows.commitment: Days to read; weeks to apply.

rows.name: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods
rows.summary: Government reference handbook on measurement, control charts, capability and reliability statistics.
rows.provider: NIST (United States National Institute of Standards and Technology) and SEMATECH
rows.accessNote: A public reference work, free to read with no account. It is a maintained handbook rather than a course.
outcomes: Look up the correct control chart and its rules for a measurement type
Compute capability and reliability statistics with the assumptions stated
Design an experiment instead of changing one factor at a time and hoping
rows.assumes: Basic statistics; the handbook introduces the rest.
rows.limits: Reference rather than teaching: excellent on method, silent on shop-floor politics and on what to do about the cause.
rows.commitment: Minutes per lookup; a week to work through one section properly.

rows.name: NIST SP 800-115: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment
rows.summary: How to plan, run and report a security assessment: review, target identification, analysis and penetration testing.
rows.accessNote: A US government publication, free to download and reuse.
outcomes: Write a test plan with scope, rules of engagement and success criteria
Distinguish a vulnerability assessment from a penetration test
Report findings so they can be acted on and then re-tested
rows.assumes: Some security background; it is written for practitioners and the managers who commission them.
rows.limits: Methodology, not technique: it will not teach you to exploit anything, and it predates some current tooling and cloud practice.
rows.commitment: A day to read; reference when planning an assessment.

rows.name: NIST SP 800-61: Incident Response Recommendations
rows.summary: The reference guide to handling a security incident in phases.
rows.accessNote: Free to download and reuse. It is written for organisations that already have an incident-response function.
outcomes: Distinguish an incident from an event and know when to escalate
Work the phases: preparation, detection, containment, recovery
Write a post-incident report that changes something
rows.assumes: Security fundamentals and some operational experience.
rows.limits: Process guidance rather than forensics: no tooling detail, and it assumes logs worth reading and an authority structure to escalate into.
rows.commitment: A day to read; a tabletop exercise to test it.

rows.name: NIST Chemistry WebBook
rows.summary: Government reference database of thermochemical, thermophysical and spectroscopic data with provenance.
rows.provider: NIST (United States National Institute of Standards and Technology)
rows.accessNote: A public reference database, free to use with no account. Cite the source and the data version when you use a value.
outcomes: Look up a property with its source and uncertainty attached
Check a simulator or handbook value against an authoritative measurement
Report where a number came from instead of quoting it bare
rows.assumes: Comfort reading data tables and knowing what properties such as enthalpy of formation mean.
rows.limits: A database rather than a course: it does not teach how to use the data, and coverage is uneven outside common compounds.
rows.commitment: Minutes per lookup; a short session to learn the search.

rows.name: NOAA National Geodetic Survey
rows.summary: The United States geodetic authority: datum definitions, control point data and conversion tools.
rows.provider: United States National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration
rows.accessNote: Free public resources including datum and coordinate tools; some services ask for a free account or an API key. This is the authority that defines the datum it serves.
outcomes: Look up the official definition of a datum and how it is realised
Retrieve control point data and understand what it certifies
Use transformation tools from the organisation that defines the reference frame
rows.assumes: Enough geodesy to know what you are asking for.
rows.limits: United States-focused and technical; it assumes you already understand the difference between a datum and a projection.
rows.commitment: Reference; 3–10 h to use the tools confidently.

rows.name: NPTEL: Embedded Systems Design (IIT)
rows.summary: Full university lecture course on embedded systems, delivered by IIT faculty.
rows.accessNote: Lectures are free to watch. An optional proctored exam and certificate are paid.
outcomes: Explain interrupts, scheduling and real-time constraints
Design firmware for a device with tight memory and power budgets
Follow a university treatment rather than a tutorial
rows.assumes: C programming and some digital logic.
rows.limits: Fixed-pacing recordings with no lab hardware, and the proctored exam is paid. It predates current toolchains in places.
rows.commitment: A semester of lectures.

rows.name: NPTEL: Renewable Energy (IIT)
rows.summary: University lecture course covering solar, wind, biomass and integration.
rows.accessNote: Lectures free; certification exam optional and paid.
outcomes: Compare solar, wind and biomass technologies honestly
Explain the grid-integration constraints that limit them
Follow a university-level treatment of energy systems
rows.assumes: Basic physics and electrical fundamentals.
rows.limits: Fixed-pacing recordings with no lab work, and the certification exam is optional and paid.
rows.commitment: A semester of lectures.

rows.name: PVGIS Solar Radiation Database
rows.summary: Free irradiance and PV yield data with a map interface and downloadable datasets.
rows.accessNote: Public data, free to use with attribution to the JRC. Coverage is strongest in Europe, Africa and Asia.
outcomes: Pull irradiance and yield data for a specific location
Compare sites and seasons with real numbers instead of assumptions
Use public data where a guess would otherwise go
rows.assumes: Basic electricity and PV vocabulary.
rows.limits: Data and tooling rather than teaching: it will not tell you how a system is designed, and coverage varies by region.
rows.commitment: Reference; an afternoon to learn the interface.

rows.name: Open Geospatial Consortium standards
rows.summary: The standards that let spatial data and services work across different software, vendors and decades.
rows.accessNote: Standards documents and community resources are free to read; some working-group participation requires organisational membership, which does not affect reading or implementing them.
outcomes: Read the standards that make spatial data interoperable
Understand what a compliance claim does and does not guarantee
Design data products that survive a change of tools
rows.assumes: Working knowledge of GIS data models.
rows.limits: Standards text is dense and written for implementers: it will not teach you to make a map, and it is not a substitute for the software documentation.
rows.commitment: Read the standards your work touches; 10–25 h.

rows.name: Onshape Learning Resources
rows.summary: Parametric CAD tutorials from a cloud CAD vendor.
rows.accessNote: Learning material is free; the software requires a free account and education plans have limits. Free documents are public by default — check before using for confidential work.
outcomes: Model parts and assemblies with a feature-based workflow
Use document versions and collaboration on CAD work
Export for manufacturing or 3D printing
rows.assumes: Nothing, but a browser and an account are mandatory.
rows.limits: A vendor platform: documents are public unless you pay, education plans have limits, and there is no offline mode.
rows.commitment: Days of tutorials; ongoing practice.

rows.name: OpenCV: Python Tutorials
rows.summary: Official tutorials for classic computer vision in Python, versioned with the library.
rows.accessNote: Free and open source with no account. The documentation is versioned, so match the tutorial to the release you installed.
outcomes: Load, transform and filter images and video programmatically
Detect features, contours and motion in a stream
Build a classical pipeline that runs without a GPU
rows.assumes: Python and basic array handling.
rows.limits: Classical computer vision: no deep learning, little calibration theory, and nothing about deploying a vision system.
rows.commitment: Days for the core tutorials; a project to consolidate.

rows.name: OpenDroneMap documentation (ODM)
rows.summary: Produce orthophotos, point clouds and 3D models from overlapping aerial images, using open-source software you run yourself.
rows.accessNote: Free, open-source documentation and software; you run it on your own machine or server. Separate from the paid hosted service some of the community offers.
outcomes: Turn a set of overlapping images into an orthophoto and a point cloud
Understand ground control, overlap and what makes photogrammetry accurate
Produce a terrain product you can measure in a GIS
rows.assumes: Comfort with Docker or a Linux shell for the standard installation.
rows.limits: Photogrammetry is only as good as the images and ground control: the documentation assumes you already have photos and know your local drone rules, including where you may not fly.
rows.commitment: A weekend to a first product; 15–40 h to do it properly.

rows.name: OpenSim: musculoskeletal modelling and simulation
rows.summary: Open-source software and models for simulating human movement and estimating joint loads.
rows.provider: Stanford University (OpenSim project, US National Center for Simulation in Rehabilitation Research)
rows.accessNote: Free and open source with published models and documentation. No account needed to download.
outcomes: Scale a musculoskeletal model to a subject and check it
Run inverse kinematics and inverse dynamics on a movement
Interpret joint moment output and state its assumptions
rows.assumes: Rigid-body mechanics, some programming, and patience with file formats.
rows.limits: Steep learning curve, community support only, and results are only as good as the motion data and marker model you feed it.
rows.commitment: Weeks to a defensible analysis.

rows.name: OpenStax: Anatomy and Physiology 2e
rows.summary: Open textbook on body systems with the structure and function detail engineers usually skip.
rows.accessNote: Openly licensed (CC BY). Free web and PDF; printed copies optional and paid.
outcomes: Name the parts and functions of the main body systems
Describe how joints, muscles and bones produce movement
Use correct anatomical terminology when discussing a device or a model
rows.assumes: School-level biology; the text starts from cell structure.
rows.limits: Descriptive anatomy and physiology: no mechanics, no quantitative modelling and no clinical training.
rows.commitment: A two-semester sequence if worked fully; use it as a reference instead.

rows.name: OpenStax: Calculus Volume 1
rows.summary: Open textbook covering limits, derivatives and integration.
rows.accessNote: Openly licensed; free online. Print copies optional.
outcomes: Compute limits, derivatives and integrals with confidence
Apply the fundamental theorem of calculus rather than memorise it
Follow a proof-based treatment instead of a recipe list
rows.assumes: Algebra, trigonometry and functions.
rows.limits: Volume 1 ends at integration techniques; series and multivariable calculus are in later volumes. Answers are in the back rather than graded.
rows.commitment: A semester-scale textbook.

rows.name: OpenStax: Chemistry 2e
rows.summary: Peer-reviewed general chemistry textbook with stoichiometry, thermochemistry and equilibrium.
rows.accessNote: Openly licensed (CC BY). Free web and PDF versions; printed copies are optional and paid.
outcomes: Use stoichiometry, limiting reagents and yields quantitatively
Calculate reaction enthalpies and reason about equilibrium shifts
Connect laboratory chemistry to the balances later used in process work
rows.assumes: School-level algebra; the book develops the chemistry from the start.
rows.limits: General chemistry only: no engineering units, no equipment and no design content.
rows.commitment: A two-semester chemistry sequence if worked as a full course.

rows.name: OpenStax: Introductory Statistics 2e
rows.summary: Applied statistics textbook, from describing data to inference.
rows.accessNote: Free to read online and download under a CC licence. No account is needed; printed copies are sold separately.
outcomes: Choose the summary measure a dataset deserves, instead of defaulting to the mean
Run the hypothesis test a question calls for and defend the choice
Interpret a confidence interval and a p-value without overclaiming
rows.assumes: Algebra; no calculus is used.
rows.limits: Applied textbook statistics: it stops short of statistical learning, and the exercises are not machine-marked.
rows.commitment: A semester textbook, or chapters as references.

rows.name: OpenStax: University Physics
rows.summary: Peer-reviewed open textbook covering mechanics through electromagnetism.
rows.accessNote: Openly licensed (CC BY). Free PDF and web versions; printed copies are optional and paid.
outcomes: Work through university-level mechanics and thermodynamics with calculus
Solve multi-step problems where the setup is the hard part
Self-check with the end-of-chapter problems
rows.assumes: Calculus, taken alongside or before it.
rows.limits: Volume 1 stops before electromagnetism (Volumes 2 and 3), and there is no laboratory component.
rows.commitment: A full-year textbook; individual chapters work as references.

rows.name: OpenTelemetry Documentation
rows.summary: Vendor-neutral standard for traces, metrics and logs, with SDKs you run yourself.
rows.accessNote: Free and open source with no account; the SDKs and the collector run locally or self-hosted. Third-party backends may charge.
outcomes: Instrument a service so its traces, metrics and logs line up
Understand why a trace answers questions metrics cannot
Export telemetry without locking your code to one vendor
rows.assumes: A service you are allowed to modify, and basic observability vocabulary.
rows.limits: Instrumentation and the specification: dashboards, alert policy and cost control are the backend’s business.
rows.commitment: Days to instrument one service properly.

rows.name: OpenTopography
rows.summary: High-resolution topography and lidar point clouds, with browser tools and APIs to get them into your analysis.
rows.accessNote: Free access to topography and lidar data with web tools and APIs; a free account raises download limits. Attribution requirements vary by data set and are stated on each.
outcomes: Find and download elevation models and lidar for a chosen area
Derive terrain products without owning any survey hardware
Read the vertical accuracy that comes attached to the data
rows.assumes: Basic raster concepts in a GIS.
rows.limits: Data access rather than instruction; coverage and resolution depend on what has been contributed, and very large areas exceed the download limits.
rows.commitment: 3–10 h to learn the tools and the catalogue.

rows.name: OSHA: Ergonomics
rows.summary: Guidance on musculoskeletal hazards at work and the workstation changes that remove them.
rows.provider: United States Occupational Safety and Health Administration
rows.accessNote: A United States government publication, free to read without an account. Note that this provider rejects automated link checkers with HTTP 403, so the app labels it “not automatically confirmed” even though the page opens normally in a browser.
outcomes: Recognise the risk factors — force, posture, repetition, vibration — in a task
Follow a simple process for evaluating and fixing a workstation
Make the case for a change in terms of injury risk rather than only output
rows.assumes: No technical background.
rows.limits: Introductory guidance without measurement methods; a full risk assessment needs a trained assessor.
rows.commitment: An hour to read; a day to apply to one workstation.

rows.name: OSHA: Machine guarding
rows.summary: The regulator’s guidance on guarding machinery, including the hazards and the control measures expected.
rows.provider: United States Occupational Safety and Health Administration
rows.accessNote: A United States government publication, free to read without an account. It states United States requirements; other countries have their own, often stricter, machinery rules. Note that this provider rejects automated link checkers with HTTP 403, so the app labels it “not automatically confirmed” even though the page opens normally in a browser.
outcomes: Name the mechanical hazards a guard must control
Recognise the difference between a guard, a device and a procedure
Ask the right questions before touching a machine or its control system
rows.assumes: No engineering background; the guidance is written for employers and workers.
rows.limits: Regulatory guidance with no design method: it tells you what must not be accessible, not how to design the cell.
rows.commitment: An hour to read with the checklists.

rows.name: OSHA: Process Safety Management standard
rows.summary: The United States regulation that defines a process safety management programme and its required elements.
rows.provider: United States Occupational Safety and Health Administration
rows.accessNote: A United States government publication, free to read without an account. It is a national legal requirement, quoted here as a reference model rather than as a legal obligation elsewhere. Note that this provider rejects automated link checkers with HTTP 403, so the app labels it “not automatically confirmed” even though the page opens normally in a browser.
outcomes: Read the elements of a formal process safety management programme
Understand what a process hazard analysis is required to cover
Recognise the management systems that sit behind equipment safeguards
rows.assumes: Familiarity with some industrial process, however simple.
rows.limits: Regulatory text: no worked examples, no calculations and written for compliance rather than learning.
rows.commitment: An afternoon to read; months to apply properly at a site.

rows.name: OWASP Juice Shop
rows.summary: Deliberately vulnerable application for practising attacks lawfully on your own machine.
rows.accessNote: Free and open source. Run it locally or in a container; only test instances you control.
outcomes: Exploit — and then fix — injection, broken access control and XSS
Read a vulnerability report and reproduce it yourself
Practise attacking something that is meant to be attacked
rows.assumes: A working Node.js or Docker setup and basic web knowledge.
rows.limits: Deliberately vulnerable software: run it locally or in an isolated container, never on a public host.
rows.commitment: Hours per challenge family; open-ended.

rows.name: OWASP Top 10
rows.summary: The reference list of the most critical web application security risks.
rows.accessNote: Free and openly licensed. No account needed.
outcomes: Name the ten risk categories and what causes each one
Map a finding from a code review or scan to a category
Read the prevention guidance for an application you maintain
rows.assumes: Basic familiarity with web applications.
rows.limits: A categorisation, not a course: it tells you what to worry about, not how to test for it. Pair it with the labs.
rows.commitment: An hour or two of reading; longer to act on.

rows.name: pandas User Guide
rows.summary: Official guide to loading, reshaping, joining and aggregating tabular data.
rows.accessNote: Free and open source documentation.
outcomes: Load, clean, reshape and join tabular data
Group and aggregate without fighting the index
Chain operations so the next reader can follow them
rows.assumes: Python basics and somewhere to run a notebook.
rows.limits: pandas only: no visualisation, no statistics, and nothing about the memory ceiling of larger-than-RAM data.
rows.commitment: Days for the user guide; reference afterwards.

rows.name: PhysioNet: physiological signal databases and tutorials
rows.summary: Large archive of real ECG, EEG, gait and other physiological records with documentation and tutorials.
rows.provider: PhysioNet (MIT Laboratory for Computational Physiology and partners)
rows.accessNote: Openly available research data with documentation. Some record sets require a data-use agreement and a training certificate, which is free but must be completed.
outcomes: Download a documented real physiological record and work with it
Follow a tutorial that goes from raw signal to a reproducible measurement
Cite the exact database and version you used
rows.assumes: Ability to read a small amount of Python and handle a file format such as WFDB.
rows.limits: Data and tutorials rather than a course: nothing here teaches physiology, and every dataset carries its own licence and citation requirement.
rows.commitment: An afternoon to the first record; weeks to a complete analysis.

rows.name: PortSwigger Web Security Academy
rows.summary: Free guided labs covering injection, access control, XSS and more.
rows.accessNote: Free labs and reading require a free account; no payment needed.
outcomes: Complete guided labs on injection, access control and authentication flaws
Use an intercepting proxy competently
Read HTTP requests and responses the way an attacker does
rows.assumes: HTTP basics and willingness to run a proxy tool.
rows.limits: Web application security only — nothing on network, endpoint or physical security, and the labs need a free account.
rows.commitment: Weeks of labs worked steadily.

rows.name: PostgreSQL Tutorial
rows.summary: Official tutorial that walks through SQL from SELECT to joins and functions.
rows.accessNote: Free official documentation under the PostgreSQL licence.
outcomes: Query, join and aggregate with standard SQL
Create tables with constraints and indexes that do something
Use functions and transactions on a real server database
rows.assumes: Basic programming or command-line familiarity for the setup steps.
rows.limits: Tutorial breadth only: performance tuning, replication and administration are documented elsewhere.
rows.commitment: A few sessions — it is a tutorial, not a course.

rows.name: Practical Cryptography for Developers
rows.summary: Developer-facing cryptography: hashes, MACs, symmetric and asymmetric encryption, key exchange and TLS, with code.
rows.accessNote: Free to read online as an open book; the code samples are openly licensed.
outcomes: Choose a hash, MAC or cipher for a stated requirement
Store passwords so that a database leak remains survivable
Explain what TLS guarantees and precisely where it stops
rows.assumes: Programming experience and comfort with basic mathematics.
rows.limits: Practical and opinionated with simplified mathematics: for an adversary who is serious, follow its advice to consult the standards it cites.
rows.commitment: A week of evenings; reference afterwards.

rows.name: The Practical Test Pyramid
rows.summary: How to split effort between unit, integration and end-to-end tests, and what each layer is actually for.
rows.accessNote: Free to read; no account, registration or newsletter.
outcomes: Decide which layer a new test belongs at
Recognise a suite that is slow, flaky or testing nothing
Argue for fewer end-to-end tests with the trade-offs in hand
rows.assumes: Having written and run some tests already.
rows.limits: Article-length strategy rather than tooling, and its examples follow one stack’s conventions.
rows.commitment: An hour to read, and worth re-reading after a project.

rows.name: Pro Git (2nd edition)
rows.summary: The standard book on Git, from basics to internals.
rows.accessNote: Free to read online under CC BY-NC-SA 3.0.
outcomes: Branch, merge and rebase without fear of losing work
Recover from mistakes with reflog, bisect and stash
Explain what a commit actually is when a colleague asks
rows.assumes: Comfort with a terminal.
rows.limits: Chapter 10 is internals and assumes a systems background. It stops at Git and says nothing about team workflow policy.
rows.commitment: A few evenings; chapters 2–3 cover most daily use.

rows.name: PROJ documentation
rows.summary: The library behind almost every coordinate transformation, documented at the level where you can verify what happened.
rows.accessNote: Free, open-source documentation. PROJ is the reference implementation used inside QGIS, GDAL and most spatial databases, so reading it explains behaviour you will meet everywhere.
outcomes: Understand transformation pipelines and the accuracy each step claims
Choose a transformation between two reference frames deliberately
Debug coordinates that land in the wrong place with evidence rather than trial and error
rows.assumes: Coordinate reference systems at working level, including datums and projections.
rows.limits: A library manual rather than a geodesy course: it tells you how to express a transformation, not which one your legal or surveying context requires.
rows.commitment: Read the sections your problem needs; 5–15 h.

rows.name: Prometheus Documentation
rows.summary: Metrics, exporters, PromQL and alerting configuration.
rows.accessNote: Free and open source.
outcomes: Instrument an application so it exposes useful metrics
Write PromQL queries and alerts that fire for the right reason
Reason about cardinality and why it bites
rows.assumes: Running services and basic HTTP.
rows.limits: Metrics only: logs, traces and long-term storage are other projects, and the docs assume you operate the server.
rows.commitment: Days; deeper once you own a service.

rows.name: pytest Documentation
rows.summary: Official guide to the most widely used Python test framework: fixtures, parametrisation, assertions and plugins.
rows.accessNote: Free and open source documentation under a permissive licence.
outcomes: Write tests whose failures tell you what broke instead of that something did
Use fixtures to set up and tear down state cleanly
Parametrise one test over many cases, and re-run only what failed
rows.assumes: Python and the idea of running a test command.
rows.limits: Python and framework specific: it teaches the tool, not what is worth testing or where a test belongs.
rows.commitment: A few evenings to be productive; reference afterwards.

rows.name: Python for Data Analysis (3rd edition)
rows.summary: The pandas book by its author, free to read online.
rows.accessNote: The complete book is free to read online; print and ebook editions are paid and add nothing to the content.
outcomes: Load messy real-world data and get it into a usable frame
Reshape, join and aggregate without fighting the index
Time a pandas operation, find the slow part and fix it
rows.assumes: Working Python.
rows.limits: pandas-centred: visualisation and modelling live in other books, and it will not teach you statistics.
rows.commitment: A few weeks of evenings; reference afterwards.

rows.name: The Python Tutorial
rows.summary: The official Python tutorial, kept current by the language maintainers.
rows.accessNote: Official documentation, free to read and reuse under the PSF licence.
outcomes: Write scripts with functions, classes, modules and exceptions
Use the standard library the way the language expects
Read the rest of the documentation unaided
rows.assumes: Some programming experience — the tutorial says so itself and is not a first-ever course.
rows.limits: No exercises and nothing graded: it teaches by example, so pair it with a practice resource.
rows.commitment: An afternoon to a weekend to read; reference afterwards.

rows.name: PyTorch Tutorials
rows.summary: Official tutorials from tensors to training and deploying models.
rows.accessNote: Free tutorials. GPU compute is not included — free notebook tiers exist but have quotas.
outcomes: Train, evaluate and save a neural network
Work with tensors, autograd, datasets and data loaders
Fine-tune an existing model instead of training from nothing
rows.assumes: Python and machine-learning basics; tensors are introduced but the pace is quick.
rows.limits: The library, not the theory — no derivations — and free GPU notebook tiers have quotas that will interrupt long runs.
rows.commitment: Days to weeks, depending how far you go.

rows.name: QGIS Training Manual
rows.summary: A structured, exercise-driven course on the same software, from first layers to finished analysis.
rows.accessNote: A complete free course with exercises and sample data sets, kept by the QGIS project. No video and no certificate; nothing to pay and nothing to sign up for.
outcomes: Follow a GIS course in order, with real data sets and expected results
Practise vector and raster operations in the sequence a project actually needs them
Build a map from raw data to a finished layout
rows.assumes: Willingness to follow the exercises in order rather than browsing.
rows.limits: A few exercises depend on sample data you must download separately, and screenshots lag the newest releases.
rows.commitment: Around 20–40 h to complete honestly rather than skim.

rows.name: QGIS Documentation: User Manual
rows.summary: The reference manual for the most widely used free desktop GIS: every tool, described with what it needs and what it produces.
rows.accessNote: Open documentation under a Creative Commons licence; no account and no cost. Use the version selector to match the manual to the release you installed, because tools move between versions.
outcomes: Load, style, label and query vector and raster layers
Reproject data and understand what the coordinate reference system selector is doing
Run spatial analysis tools and compose a print layout you can hand to somebody
rows.assumes: No prior GIS experience; basic file handling.
rows.limits: Reference documentation rather than a teaching sequence: it answers “how do I do this” and assumes you bring the question.
rows.commitment: Use as a reference; 10–25 h of working through the sections your project needs.

rows.name: React: Learn
rows.summary: Official React tutorial and concept documentation.
rows.accessNote: Free official documentation under an open licence.
outcomes: Build an interface from components with state and props
Handle lists, forms, effects and errors correctly
Avoid the standard traps: keys, stale state, effect dependencies
rows.assumes: Solid JavaScript — arrow functions, destructuring, modules — plus HTML and CSS.
rows.limits: React itself: routing, data fetching and build tooling live on separate pages and are not introduced here.
rows.commitment: Days for the tutorial; reference afterwards.

rows.name: React Native Documentation
rows.summary: Build a mobile app from React components, reusing concepts that carry over from the web.
rows.provider: Meta and the React Native community
rows.accessNote: Free and open source. The toolchain costs nothing; building for iOS needs a Mac, and store accounts cost money.
outcomes: Compose a mobile interface from native components with navigation
Use platform APIs — storage, camera, notifications — from JavaScript
Run and debug the same code on iOS and Android emulators
rows.assumes: React and JavaScript; the tutorial does not reteach them.
rows.limits: One route to cross-platform mobile. Anything genuinely native still needs platform languages, and graphics-heavy apps struggle.
rows.commitment: Days for the basics; a real app to become fluent.

rows.name: Refactoring Guru: Design Patterns
rows.summary: Every classic design pattern with the problem it solves, its structure, and code in several languages.
rows.accessNote: The catalogue is free to read with no account. Ebooks and courses are paid; the free pages are complete on their own.
outcomes: Name the pattern you are already using, so you can explain it
Choose between two similar patterns and say why one fits
Recognise a pattern applied where it adds nothing
rows.assumes: Comfort in at least one object-oriented language.
rows.limits: Patterns described largely apart from the systems that produce them: nothing on architecture at service level, nothing on testing the result.
rows.commitment: Reference; a weekend read end to end.

rows.name: Reliable Plant: maintenance and reliability library
rows.summary: Practitioner articles and case studies on maintenance strategy, reliability and condition monitoring.
rows.accessNote: Articles are free to read; the publisher also sells training and consulting, so the free library is the resource and the rest is optional and paid.
outcomes: Read how maintenance decisions are actually made in plants
Find a worked example of a reliability improvement
Pick up the vocabulary used by maintenance teams
rows.assumes: Some exposure to industrial equipment.
rows.limits: Vendor-published practitioner material: useful and practical, but not peer-reviewed and with an interest in selling training.
rows.commitment: Minutes per article.

rows.name: RESNA: Rehabilitation Engineering and Assistive Technology Society of North America
rows.summary: Professional body for assistive technology practitioners, with public standards and practice information.
rows.accessNote: Public pages, position papers and standards information are free to read. Membership, certification and conference access are paid and are not needed for the public material.
outcomes: See how assistive technology practice is organised and certified
Find the standards that apply to wheelchairs, seating and other products
Know where practitioners publish and discuss the work
rows.assumes: Some familiarity with disability services and assistive products.
rows.limits: A society rather than a course: much of the technical material sits behind membership or conference fees.
rows.commitment: Reference use.

rows.name: Robot Academy (QUT): free robotics and automation lectures
rows.summary: Short university lectures on robotics, kinematics and control, aimed at working engineers.
rows.accessNote: Free to watch, no account required, produced as an open educational resource by the university.
outcomes: Get a rigorous but short explanation of kinematics, sensing or control
See the mathematics behind a robot cell rather than a vendor demonstration
Link automation theory to the software that runs real machines
rows.assumes: Linear algebra and some programming for the later lectures.
rows.limits: Robotics-focused: it does not cover PLC programming standards, safety circuits or factory planning.
rows.commitment: Ten to thirty minutes per lecture.

rows.name: ROS 2 Documentation
rows.summary: Official tutorials for nodes, topics, services, transforms and simulation.
rows.accessNote: Free and open source documentation.
outcomes: Write a node that publishes, subscribes and calls a service
Use parameters, launch files and coordinate transforms
Run a robot in simulation and inspect what it is doing
rows.assumes: Python or C++, Linux comfort, and a workspace you can build.
rows.limits: Framework documentation: it does not teach robotics theory, and it assumes your sensors and robot already exist or are simulated.
rows.commitment: Days for the tutorial track.

rows.name: scikit-learn User Guide
rows.summary: Practical machine-learning guide: preprocessing, models, evaluation, pipelines.
rows.accessNote: Free and open source.
outcomes: Build a pipeline that preprocesses, trains and evaluates
Choose between models and justify the choice
Find leakage and overfitting in your own experiment
rows.assumes: Python and basic statistics; the tutorials supply the numpy.
rows.limits: Classical machine learning on tidy tabular data. Deep learning, text and images are elsewhere.
rows.commitment: Days; treat it as reference plus tutorials.

rows.name: Seeing Theory
rows.summary: Interactive visual introduction to probability and statistics.
rows.accessNote: Free interactive visualisations with no account. The accompanying text is shorter than a textbook chapter.
outcomes: See what a distribution, a sample or a p-value actually does
Build intuition for correlation, regression and Bayesian updating
Explain a statistical idea to someone else using the visual
rows.assumes: School algebra.
rows.limits: Intuition, not a course: there are no derivations and no exercises, so it cannot stand in for a textbook.
rows.commitment: An hour for the first chapters; revisit each as you meet it.

rows.name: SPC for Excel: statistical process control knowledge base
rows.summary: Practitioner articles explaining control charts, capability and measurement systems with worked examples.
rows.accessNote: The knowledge base articles are free to read. The site sells spreadsheet add-ins, so treat the free articles as the resource and the software as optional and paid.
outcomes: Get a plain-language explanation of a chart rule you have to apply at work
See a worked example with real numbers rather than a formula alone
Check your interpretation of a capability index against a practitioner source
rows.assumes: Comfort with basic statistics and spreadsheets.
rows.limits: Vendor-maintained material with commercial intent: methods are sound, but it is not independent academic reference and it stops where the add-in starts.
rows.commitment: Minutes per article.

rows.name: SQLite documentation
rows.summary: Complete SQL reference plus a tutorial using a database with no server to install.
rows.accessNote: Public domain documentation, free to reuse.
outcomes: Write SQL confidently: filtering, joins, grouping, window functions
Design a small schema and understand what its constraints enforce
Practise SQL without installing a database server
rows.assumes: Nothing — the tutorial starts from SELECT.
rows.limits: The SQLite dialect, not a server database: concurrency, roles and access control are out of scope.
rows.commitment: A weekend for the tutorial and the SQL reference.

rows.name: TensorFlow / Keras Tutorials
rows.summary: Guided notebooks for classical ML, deep learning and transfer learning.
rows.accessNote: Free tutorials and open-source library.
outcomes: Build and train models with Keras
Use input pipelines and transfer learning
Export a trained model for serving elsewhere
rows.assumes: Python and machine-learning basics.
rows.limits: Framework-specific: concepts transfer, code does not. Substantial GPU or TPU time is not free beyond limited quotas.
rows.commitment: Days; reference afterwards.

rows.name: Terraform Tutorials
rows.summary: Hands-on track for describing infrastructure as code.
rows.accessNote: The tutorials and the CLI are free; a free account is needed for some tracks. HashiCorp’s hosted platforms are paid, and every tutorial here can be followed with local providers.
outcomes: Describe infrastructure in a file and apply it safely
Read a plan and spot the line that will destroy something
Manage state deliberately, and know why it must not be shared carelessly
rows.assumes: Command-line comfort and some cloud vocabulary.
rows.limits: One tool: it teaches Terraform rather than cloud architecture, and team process and secrets handling only get the basics.
rows.commitment: A weekend of tutorials, then a real project to make it stick.

rows.name: The Things Network Documentation
rows.summary: How connected sensors actually get online: LoRaWAN, gateways, payload formats and the network-server model.
rows.accessNote: Documentation is free and open. Using a community network is free to start, with fair-use expectations rather than a hard paywall.
outcomes: Explain what LoRaWAN is for, and when not to use it
Register a device and move a payload through a community network
Reason about range, duty cycle and power budget for a real deployment
rows.assumes: Basic electronics and some programming; networking helps.
rows.limits: One technology family, on a network other people operate: cellular IoT, Wi-Fi provisioning and MQTT brokers are separate worlds.
rows.commitment: Days to get a device talking end to end.

rows.name: TypeScript Handbook
rows.summary: Official guide to TypeScript types, generics and configuration.
rows.accessNote: Free official documentation.
outcomes: Write types for functions, generics, unions and object shapes
Narrow types safely instead of casting your way past errors
Configure tsconfig deliberately for a real project
rows.assumes: JavaScript you can already write.
rows.limits: It documents the type system, not application design, and assumes you have a compiler and editor set up.
rows.commitment: Days for a working read; reference afterwards.

rows.name: USGS National Geospatial Program
rows.summary: The United States national mapping programme: elevation, hydrography, imagery and land cover data with documented accuracy.
rows.accessNote: A United States government programme page: the data and products are free, and most United States government data is public domain. Coverage is strongest over the United States.
outcomes: Find authoritative elevation, hydrography and imagery data rather than scraping it
Understand what a national mapping programme publishes and why
Identify data whose accuracy is documented by the producer
rows.assumes: None beyond basic computer literacy; the pages are written for a general reader.
rows.limits: United States coverage and conventions dominate, so other countries need their own portals; the page is a programme overview rather than a tutorial.
rows.commitment: Use as a data source; 2–8 h to learn the catalogue.

rows.name: WHO: Assistive technology fact sheet
rows.summary: World Health Organization summary of who needs assistive technology, what exists and what is missing.
rows.accessNote: Public fact sheet from an international agency, free to read without an account.
outcomes: Understand the scale of unmet need for assistive products
Name the categories of assistive product and who they serve
Frame a design problem in terms of function and access rather than novelty
rows.assumes: No technical background.
rows.limits: An overview, not a design guide: no engineering detail and no costed solutions.
rows.commitment: Fifteen minutes to read.

rows.name: Fundamentals of Data Visualization
rows.summary: How to choose a chart and design it honestly: colour, scales, proportions, and the failure modes of each chart type.
rows.accessNote: Free to read online under a CC BY-NC-ND licence; the print edition is optional and paid.
outcomes: Choose a chart type because of the data, not because of the tool
Fix colour, axes and labels so a chart stops misleading
Critique a published figure and say precisely what is wrong with it
rows.assumes: Basic statistics and some experience plotting data; the examples use R but the reasoning transfers.
rows.limits: Design and communication rather than analysis: no statistics, and interactive or animated visualisation is out of scope.
rows.commitment: A book; a few weeks of evenings.

rows.name: Wireshark User’s Guide
rows.summary: Official manual for capturing and filtering packets, following streams and reading protocols at the wire level.
rows.accessNote: Free and open source; no account needed for the manual or the software.
outcomes: Capture traffic on an interface and filter it down to what matters
Follow a TCP stream and explain a handshake, a retransmission or a reset
Recognise an anomalous pattern in traffic you are lawfully capturing
rows.assumes: Network basics: layers, ports, protocols.
rows.limits: A tool manual rather than a security course. It teaches you to see packets, not to interpret an attack — and capture legality is your responsibility.
rows.commitment: A weekend to be genuinely useful with it; reference afterwards.
