  n.estimatedHoursLow = row.estimatedHoursLow,
  n.mustBeSelfReported = row.mustBeSelfReported,
  n.name = row.name,
  n.practice = row.practice,
  n.summary = row.summary,
  n.tags = row.tags,
  n.verification = row.verification

rows.name: Aerodynamics basics
rows.summary: Lift, drag, Reynolds number and basic wing behaviour.
rows.description: Aerodynamics explains why a wing works and why it stalls. It relies on fluid mechanics plus careful attention to non-dimensional numbers.
practice: Compute lift for a given wing area and coefficient, then sanity-check the result.
Explain in a paragraph why stall happens as angle of attack increases.
completionCriteria: You can estimate lift and drag for a simple wing.
You can explain the role of Reynolds number in wind-tunnel scaling.

rows.name: Algorithms in practice
rows.summary: Sorting, searching, graphs, dynamic programming and how to apply them.
rows.description: Beyond the data structure: which algorithmic approach fits which problem, and how to test that it is fast enough on real input sizes.
practice: Implement breadth-first search for a maze and measure it on a large map.
Compare two solutions to the same problem and benchmark them on increasing input.
completionCriteria: You can pick a strategy (greedy, divide-and-conquer, DP) and explain why.
You can benchmark and improve a solution that is too slow.

rows.name: Analog electronics
rows.summary: Diodes, transistors, op-amps, filters and noise.
rows.description: Real signals are analog before they are digital. Amplifiers, filtering and noise control decide whether a measurement is usable.
practice: Design and simulate a non-inverting amplifier for a specified gain.
Measure noise on a sensor line and propose one mitigation you can justify.
completionCriteria: You can design a simple amplifier stage and explain component choices.
You can describe what limits your measurement accuracy.

rows.name: API design and integration
rows.summary: HTTP, REST basics, authentication, versioning and error handling.
rows.description: APIs are contracts. Designing predictable endpoints and handling failures gracefully is what separates a demo from a product.
practice: Design and implement three endpoints with validation and consistent error bodies.
Write a client that retries safely and surfaces errors to the user.
completionCriteria: Your API returns useful, non-leaky error responses.
You can explain idempotency for at least one endpoint.

rows.name: Applied cryptography
rows.summary: Hashing, symmetric and asymmetric encryption, TLS, and how to use libraries correctly.
rows.description: Use standard libraries, never invent algorithms, and always ask what property you need: confidentiality, integrity or authentication. Key management is usually the hard part.
practice: Store passwords with a proper KDF and verify them, then explain why hashing alone is not enough.
Inspect a TLS certificate chain and explain each field’s role.
completionCriteria: You can choose an appropriate primitive for a stated security property.
You can explain the difference between hashing, encryption and signing.

rows.name: Assistive and rehabilitation technology
rows.summary: Devices that restore function, designed with the people who will use them rather than for them.
rows.description: Assistive technology only works if it fits a real body, a real routine and a real budget. You learn user-centred design with disabled users, prosthetics and orthotics basics, seating and mobility, and how to evaluate a device on function achieved rather than on engineering elegance.
practice: Interview or observe one assistive device in use and document three failures a designer would not have predicted.
Propose a modification and define how you would measure whether it helped.
completionCriteria: You can describe a device’s limitations from the user’s perspective, not the spec sheet.
You can state which outcome measure you would use and why it is the right one.

rows.name: Biomaterials and biocompatibility
rows.summary: Choosing a material that the body will tolerate, and proving it will not fail quietly.
rows.description: Inside the body, metals corrode, polymers release additives and every surface provokes a response. You work with the material classes used in implants, corrosion and wear mechanisms, sterilisation effects, and the tests that stand in for years of service.
practice: Compare three candidate materials for one implant application on strength, corrosion and cost, and pick one.
Design a screening test that would reject a bad surface finish before an animal study.
completionCriteria: You can explain why a material that is inert in air may not be inert in tissue.
You can name the failure mode you were most worried about and how you tested for it.

rows.name: Biomechanics
rows.summary: Statics and dynamics of the body: joint loads, gait, and what a replacement part has to survive.
rows.description: The human body is a mechanism with unusual materials. You estimate forces at joints from free-body diagrams, examine gait cycles and ground reaction forces, and learn why an implant’s loading history, not just its strength, decides whether it survives.
practice: Estimate the knee joint reaction force in a single-leg stance from a free-body diagram and state your assumptions.
Break one gait cycle into phases and say which muscles and moments dominate each phase.
completionCriteria: You can defend a simplified body model, including what it leaves out.
You can describe the load cycle an implant sees over a million steps.

rows.name: Biomedical signals and instrumentation
rows.summary: Acquiring tiny physiological signals safely: electrodes, amplifiers, filtering and patient isolation.
rows.description: An ECG is a millivolt signal on a body that is also a conductor sitting in a room full of mains wiring. You learn electrode behaviour, differential amplification, common-mode rejection, bandwidth and anti-alias filtering, and the electrical safety rules that decide what may be connected to a person at all.
practice: Take one public ECG record, remove baseline wander and mains interference, and show the before and after.
Calculate the common-mode rejection you need to keep mains hum below the amplitude of the signal you want.
completionCriteria: You can explain why a differential amplifier is used instead of a better single-ended one.
You can state the isolation and leakage-current limits that apply before anything touches a patient.

rows.name: CAD 3D modelling
rows.summary: Creating parametric 3D models, assemblies and manufacturing drawings.
rows.description: CAD is the working language of design. Being parametric matters more than memorising buttons: dimensions should drive the model so revisions do not break it.
practice: Model a bracket parametrically so changing one hole diameter updates the whole part.
Create a two-part assembly with mates and export a dimensioned drawing.
completionCriteria: You can edit a dimension and have the model update without errors.
You can produce a drawing another person could manufacture from.

rows.name: Calculus for engineering
rows.summary: Differentiation, integration and simple differential equations applied to physical systems.
rows.description: Beyond the basics: rates of change in dynamic systems, accumulation, and first-order differential equations that describe capacitors, cooling and populations.
practice: Model the charging of a capacitor with a first-order ODE and solve it by hand.
Compare a numerical integration with an analytical solution for a simple function.
completionCriteria: You can set up the differential equation for a first-order physical system and solve it.
You can explain why numerical methods are needed for most real systems.

rows.name: CI/CD pipelines
rows.summary: Automated build, test and deployment with quality gates.
rows.description: Automation is what makes quality repeatable. The pipeline should fail loudly on a broken test and deploy honestly, with rollback in mind.
practice: Add a pipeline that lints, tests and builds on every push.
Add a deployment stage gated on tests passing, with a rollback note.
completionCriteria: A failing test blocks your deployment.
You documented how to roll back.

rows.name: Circuit analysis
rows.summary: Ohm’s law, Kirchhoff’s laws, series/parallel networks and the basics of AC.
rows.description: The first real engineering analysis most students do. Thevenin equivalents and node/mesh analysis are tools you will reuse for years.
practice: Solve a two-loop network with both node and mesh analysis and confirm the same answer.
Measure a real resistive divider and compare with your calculated values.
completionCriteria: You can analyse a resistive network without a simulator.
You can explain your measured versus calculated discrepancy.

rows.name: Cloud fundamentals
rows.summary: Compute, storage, networking and cost models in shared cloud infrastructure.
rows.description: Cloud is someone else’s computer with an API and a bill. Understand regions, identity, network boundaries and how to avoid surprise costs.
practice: Deploy a small service and set a budget alert with a hard limit.
Compare running locally versus in the cloud on cost and complexity, with numbers.
completionCriteria: You can describe every resource you created and its cost driver.
You clean up resources you are not using.

rows.name: Computer networks
rows.summary: IP addressing, TCP/UDP, DNS, HTTP, routing and troubleshooting.
rows.description: Networks explain why your service is unreachable. Learn the layers, then learn to diagnose with the tools (ping, dig, curl, packet capture).
practice: Diagnose a deliberately broken network configuration using command-line tools.
Capture traffic to a local service and identify the handshake.
completionCriteria: You can explain a request’s path from browser to server and back.
You can debug a connectivity problem methodically.

rows.name: Computer vision basics
rows.summary: Images as arrays, filtering, features and modern detection pipelines.
rows.description: Vision is how many robots and products perceive. Start with classic operations, then use pretrained models before training your own.
practice: Detect a coloured object in a live camera feed with a documented threshold strategy.
Evaluate a pretrained detector on ten of your own images.
completionCriteria: You can explain why your detector fails in specific lighting conditions.
You can state your pipeline’s latency on your hardware.

rows.name: Containers and Docker
rows.summary: Images, containers, volumes, networking and reproducible environments.
rows.description: Containers remove “works on my machine”. Learn to write a small image, keep it secure and reproduce a full stack locally.
practice: Containerise an application with a multi-stage build under 200 MB.
Run a two-service stack with a volume and verify data persists across restarts.
completionCriteria: Your image runs with a non-root user and no secrets baked in.
You can explain image layers and why build order matters.

rows.name: Control systems fundamentals
rows.summary: Feedback, transfer functions, stability and PID tuning.
rows.description: Control is what makes machines behave. You will model a system, close a loop, and tune it without chasing oscillation forever.
practice: Model a DC motor as a first-order system and simulate a proportional controller.
Tune a PID on a simulated plant and record settling time for three tunings.
completionCriteria: You can explain why a system oscillates or goes unstable.
You can tune a PID loop to meet a stated settling-time target in simulation.

rows.name: Cybersecurity fundamentals
rows.summary: Threat models, the CIA triad, common attack classes and defensive basics.
rows.description: Security starts with asking what you are protecting and from whom. Learn the standard attack classes and the corresponding controls before touching tools.
practice: Write a threat model for a small application you built, listing assets and threats.
Map five OWASP Top 10 categories to concrete controls.
completionCriteria: You can produce a threat model with realistic assets and threats.
You can explain a control’s cost and its residual risk.

rows.name: Data analysis and pandas
rows.summary: Loading, cleaning, joining, grouping and summarising tabular data.
rows.description: Real data is dirty. Most analysis time is spent cleaning and validating, so learn to do it reproducibly.
practice: Clean a public dataset: fix types, handle missing values, document each decision.
Produce three summary tables that answer three questions.
completionCriteria: Your analysis script runs end to end from raw data to output.
You documented every cleaning decision and its effect.

rows.name: Data structures and algorithms
rows.summary: Arrays, lists, stacks, queues, trees, graphs, searching, sorting and complexity.
rows.description: How data is organised decides how fast programs run. This is also the standard interview currency for software roles, so learn to reason about complexity, not just implement.
practice: Implement a queue using two stacks and explain the complexity of each operation.
Solve three problems and state the time and space complexity of each solution.
completionCriteria: You can choose an appropriate structure for a problem and justify it.
You can estimate the runtime of your solution for a given input size.

rows.name: Data visualisation and communication
rows.summary: Choosing the right chart and writing the sentence it supports.
rows.description: A chart exists to support a claim. Axis honesty, appropriate chart type and a written takeaway matter more than styling.
practice: Take one dataset and produce a good and a deliberately misleading chart, then explain the difference.
Write a five-sentence summary of a chart for a non-technical reader.
completionCriteria: Your charts are readable without the source data.
You can state the claim each chart supports.

rows.name: Databases and SQL
rows.summary: Relational modelling, SQL queries, indexes and transactions.
rows.description: Most applications are mostly data. Learn to model tables and keys, then write queries that stay fast as the data grows.
practice: Design a normalised schema for a small application and write five queries against it.
Explain a query plan and add an index that improves it measurably.
completionCriteria: You can design a schema in third normal form and justify each key.
You can write a join across three tables without a reference.

rows.name: Deep learning basics
rows.summary: Neural networks, training loops, regularisation and transfer learning.
rows.description: Neural networks are a flexible function approximator with real pitfalls. Start with small datasets, then use transfer learning rather than training from scratch.
practice: Train a small network on a toy dataset and demonstrate overfitting, then reduce it.
Fine-tune a pretrained image model and report the confusion matrix.
completionCriteria: You can explain what each hyperparameter you changed actually did.
You can diagnose overfitting from the learning curves.

rows.name: Digital logic design
rows.summary: Boolean algebra, combinational and sequential circuits, timing basics.
rows.description: From truth tables to flip-flops: how logic gates become counters, state machines and eventually processors.
practice: Minimise a 4-variable logic function and build it in a simulator.
Design a 3-state traffic-light state machine and test all transitions.
completionCriteria: You can convert a specification into a state diagram and then into gates.
You can explain setup and hold time in plain language.

rows.name: Embedded C and microcontrollers
rows.summary: Memory-mapped peripherals, interrupts, timers, GPIO and constrained debugging.
rows.description: Embedded programming is C with hardware attached. Interrupts, timing and memory limits shape every design decision.
practice: Blink an LED using a timer interrupt rather than a delay loop.
Debug a program that fails only when interrupts are enabled and explain the race.
completionCriteria: You can write interrupt-safe code with volatile and atomic flags.
You can read a microcontroller datasheet to find a register.

rows.name: IoT connectivity and protocols
rows.summary: MQTT, HTTP polling, Wi-Fi and LoRa trade-offs, payload design and security.
rows.description: Connected devices must trade bandwidth, power and reliability. Security basics (TLS, credentials per device) are non-negotiable.
practice: Publish sensor data over MQTT with a per-device credential and reconnect handling.
Compare power use of continuous Wi-Fi versus periodic transmission.
completionCriteria: Your device recovers from a dropped connection without losing data.
No shared or hard-coded credentials exist in your firmware.

rows.name: Energy auditing and efficiency
rows.summary: Measuring consumption, identifying waste and costing improvements.
rows.description: Efficiency work starts with measurement. Find the largest loads, quantify waste and rank improvements by cost and saving.
practice: Audit one building or lab: measure, tabulate and rank five improvements.
Estimate payback for the top recommendation and state its uncertainty.
completionCriteria: Your recommendations are ranked by measured impact, not intuition.
Each recommendation includes a cost estimate.

rows.name: Engineering materials
rows.summary: Metals, polymers, ceramics, composites: choosing material by property, not habit.
rows.description: Material choice decides weight, cost, corrosion behaviour and failure mode. You will compare stiffness, strength, toughness and manufacturability for real components.
practice: Choose a material for a bicycle frame using strength-to-weight ratios and justify the choice.
Compare two candidate materials for a corrosion-prone part and state the trade-offs.
completionCriteria: You can justify a material choice with numbers rather than preference.
You can name the dominant failure mode for the material you chose.

rows.name: Engineering mathematics
rows.summary: Algebra, trigonometry, functions and the calculus used in every engineering subject.
rows.description: The shared language of engineering. You need enough fluency to rearrange equations, work with trigonometric identities and understand a rate of change, because mechanics, circuits and control all assume it.
practice: Solve five mechanics problems that require rearranging an equation before substituting numbers.
Sketch the derivative of three real signals (a ramp, a sine and a step).
completionCriteria: You can rearrange a multi-variable equation for any variable without guessing.
You can explain what a derivative means physically in two different engineering contexts.

rows.name: Statics and equilibrium
rows.summary: Forces, moments, trusses and beams in equilibrium.
rows.description: Statics answers “will it hold?” The method is always the same: isolate the body, resolve forces, take moments, solve. Trusses and beams are the standard exercises.
practice: Analyse a 5-member truss for member forces using the method of joints.
Draw shear-force and bending-moment diagrams for a simply supported beam with a point load.
completionCriteria: You can find every reaction force in a static structure with two supports.
You can sketch a bending-moment diagram and explain its shape.

rows.name: Fluid mechanics basics
rows.summary: Pressure, flow, continuity, Bernoulli and losses in pipes.
rows.description: Pumps, ducts, hydraulics and aerodynamics all rest on the same few relations. Learn continuity and Bernoulli first, then friction losses.
practice: Estimate the flow rate through a pipe of known diameter and pressure difference.
Calculate head loss in a pipe run and compare it with the available pump head.
completionCriteria: You can apply continuity and Bernoulli to a real system with a sketch.
You can explain where energy is lost in a fluid system.

rows.name: Geodesy, datums and coordinate systems
rows.summary: Reference frames, projections and transformations: why coordinates must carry their datum, and how to move between them correctly.
rows.description: The choice of ellipsoid, datum and projection changes every position, distance and area you compute. You work with geographic and projected coordinates, grid versus ground distances, scale factors, and the transformation problem that appears when two data sets disagree by a few metres and both call themselves correct.
practice: Take one location in two datums or projections and compute how far apart the answers land on the ground.
Reproject a data set and compare distances and areas before and after.
completionCriteria: You can explain why vector data without a coordinate reference system is useless rather than merely imprecise.
You can say why a transformation between datums is looked up and verified, never guessed.

rows.name: Geospatial data quality and standards
rows.summary: Metadata, accuracy, topology and interoperability: why spatial data outlives the tools that made it.
rows.description: Spatial data is expensive to make and easy to ruin, so it moves between organisations under standards and licences. You learn metadata that means something, positional and attribute accuracy, data quality elements, topology and validity checks, the common exchange formats, and the open standards that let two systems understand each other ten years from now.
practice: Write a metadata record for a data set you produced and audit one you obtained from elsewhere.
Run validity and topology checks on a polygon layer and fix what fails.
completionCriteria: You can tell an accuracy statement from an accuracy claim and give an example of each.
You can explain what a standard buys you that a file format does not.

rows.name: GIS and spatial analysis
rows.summary: Vector and raster data, joins, overlays and the projection pitfalls that quietly make good analysis wrong.
rows.description: A GIS is where spatial questions become answerable: which parcels intersect a flood zone, how far the nearest school is, what changed between two dates. You learn the two fundamental data models, attribute and spatial joins, buffers, overlays and selections, map layout — and the coordinate-system mistakes that produce a confident wrong answer.
practice: Answer three spatial questions about your own neighbourhood from open data.
Run the same distance analysis in two coordinate systems and explain where the difference comes from.
completionCriteria: You can choose vector or raster for a question and defend the choice.
You can look at a finished map and say what its scale and projection hide.

rows.name: GNSS positioning
rows.summary: How satellite positioning actually works, why a phone is not a survey instrument, and what correction changes.
rows.description: Global navigation satellite systems derive position from ranges and timing, so their error is geometric as much as electronic. You learn the constellation and the signal, dilution of precision, multipath and atmospheric delay, the difference between standalone, differential and real-time kinematic positioning, and what must be true before a GNSS position is survey-grade.
practice: Log a static GNSS record and analyse its scatter, then repeat under tree cover or between buildings.
Compare a GNSS-derived position against a known point and report the error in the right units.
completionCriteria: You can explain why a perfect signal with poor satellite geometry still gives a poor position.
You can say what a correction service upgrades and what it cannot fix.

rows.name: Heat transfer
rows.summary: Conduction, convection and radiation applied to exchanger duty, insulation and cooling.
rows.description: The transport side of thermal design: resistances in series, overall heat-transfer coefficients, log-mean temperature difference, fouling margins, and why a real exchanger rarely behaves like the datasheet. It is also the reason a plant has a cooling water system at all.
practice: Size a shell-and-tube exchanger for a stated duty and check the result against a manufacturer catalogue.
Calculate the surface temperature of an insulated pipe and compare it with the safety limit you were given.
completionCriteria: You can explain a sizing as a resistance network instead of reciting a formula.
You state the fouling assumption you used and what it costs in surface area.

rows.name: Incident response basics
rows.summary: Preparation, detection, containment, eradication, recovery and lessons learned.
rows.description: When something breaks, process matters. Prepare contact paths and backups beforehand; document decisions under pressure afterwards.
practice: Write a one-page incident runbook for a service you run.
Run a tabletop exercise for a simulated ransomware event and record decisions.
completionCriteria: You have a written runbook with escalation contacts.
You can describe containment options and their trade-offs.

rows.name: Industrial automation and PLC logic
rows.summary: Machine control, interlocks and safety circuits — and the difference between what works and what is safe.
rows.description: Automation is logic plus the physical world: sensors that lie, actuators that stick, and people who will eventually reach into the machine. You learn ladder logic and state machines for control, the separation between control and safety functions, and why a simulation is the only responsible place to start.
practice: Write and simulate a conveyor interlock with a start/stop chain and an emergency stop.
List the failure modes of your own logic and say which ones need a hard-wired safeguard.
completionCriteria: You can explain why a software interlock is not a substitute for a safety-rated circuit.
You can describe what happens in your logic when a sensor sticks at its last value.

rows.name: Infrastructure as code
rows.summary: Declarative provisioning, state, reviewable changes and drift.
rows.description: If infrastructure is typed by hand it cannot be reviewed or reproduced. Declarative definitions plus version control make environments reproducible.
practice: Define a small environment declaratively and recreate it from scratch.
Show a plan output and explain what would change.
completionCriteria: You can recreate your environment from the repository alone.
You review plan output before applying changes.

rows.name: Land surveying and error budgets
rows.summary: Measuring ground positions and heights, then proving the result is good enough: traverses, levelling, closures and accuracy standards.
rows.description: Surveying is applied error management. You learn how instruments measure angles, distances and height differences, how a traverse or levelling loop is computed and adjusted, how misclosure is judged against a standard rather than a feeling, and how a set of measurements becomes a coordinate with an uncertainty attached to it.
practice: Run a closed traverse or levelling loop over a small site and compute the misclosure and adjustment.
Convert a set of manual measurements into coordinates and state the accuracy you are prepared to defend.
completionCriteria: You can state what a closure check proves and what it does not prove.
You can explain why a precise instrument does not rescue a badly designed survey.

rows.name: Linear algebra
rows.summary: Vectors, matrices, transformations and eigenvalues — the mathematics behind graphics, robotics and ML.
rows.description: Matrices describe transformations in space and systems of equations. Robotics kinematics, computer graphics and machine learning all reuse the same operations.
practice: Rotate a 2D point by 30° using a matrix and verify the result geometrically.
Solve a 3×3 linear system by elimination and by matrix inverse, then compare.
completionCriteria: You can explain what a matrix multiplication does to a shape.
You can compute an eigenvalue for a simple 2×2 matrix and say what it means.

rows.name: Low-power design
rows.summary: Sleep modes, duty cycling, power budgeting and measurement.
rows.description: Battery life is a design constraint, not a feature. Measure current, budget energy, then sleep aggressively.
practice: Measure current draw of a device in active and sleep modes with an inline meter.
Compute a battery life estimate and validate it with a 24-hour test.
completionCriteria: You can produce a power budget with measured numbers.
Your estimate and measurement are within a stated margin.

rows.name: Machine learning fundamentals
rows.summary: Supervised learning, train/validation/test discipline, baselines and evaluation metrics.
rows.description: The core loop: define the task, split the data honestly, build a baseline, train a model, evaluate on held-out data, and inspect the errors.
practice: Train two models on the same dataset, including a trivial baseline, and compare.
Write an error analysis listing the five worst predictions and possible causes.
completionCriteria: You never evaluate on training data and can explain why it matters.
You can justify your evaluation metric for the problem at hand.

rows.name: Maintenance and reliability engineering
rows.summary: Making failure predictable: failure modes, preventive and predictive maintenance, and spares policy.
rows.description: Equipment fails in patterns, and some of those patterns reward waiting while others punish it. You learn failure modes and effects analysis, mean time between failures, condition monitoring and the economics that decide whether to replace, inspect or run to failure — with the safety case on top.
practice: Run a failure-modes exercise on one machine and rank the modes by consequence and detectability.
Decide a maintenance policy for three components with different failure patterns and justify each.
completionCriteria: You can say why a scheduled replacement can increase failures for some components.
You can state what a condition-monitoring system must measure to be worth installing.

rows.name: Manufacturing and tolerances
rows.summary: Machining, joining, fits and design for manufacture.
rows.description: A drawing that cannot be made is not a design. This skill covers tolerance stacks, surface finish, standard fits, and designing parts that a workshop can actually produce at a sane cost.
practice: Calculate a tolerance stack-up for a three-part assembly and state the resulting clearance range.
Redesign a part to remove an unnecessary tight tolerance and explain the cost saving.
completionCriteria: You can specify tolerances that match the required function, not the machine’s best possible.
You can explain one manufacturing method and its design constraints.

rows.name: Manufacturing systems and lean thinking
rows.summary: Flow, takt, pull and the seven wastes — improving the system rather than pushing harder.
rows.description: Lean is a measurement discipline, not a set of posters. You calculate takt time from demand, map a value stream, find where the work waits, distinguish a bottleneck from a busy station, and pick improvements by their effect on flow instead of by how visible they are.
practice: Map the value stream for a process you can observe and mark every point where work waits.
Calculate takt time for a stated demand and compare it with your measured cycle times.
completionCriteria: You can say which station constrains the whole line, and why.
You can propose an improvement and predict its effect on throughput before you make it.

rows.name: Mass transfer and separation processes
rows.summary: Distillation, absorption, extraction, drying and membranes — and how to choose between them.
rows.description: Separations consume most of a plant’s energy and a large share of its capital. You learn staged and rate-based methods, reflux and stage efficiency, solvent selection, and the trade-offs that decide whether a column, a membrane or a crystalliser is the right answer.
practice: Design a binary distillation column to a stated purity and calculate reflux ratio and stage count.
Compare two separation routes for the same duty on energy, capital and complexity.
completionCriteria: You can explain why the reflux ratio you chose is not simply the minimum.
You can defend a separation choice against two alternatives with numbers.

rows.name: Material and energy balances
rows.summary: Accounting for every kilogram and every joule that crosses a process boundary.
rows.description: The first real process skill. You pick a control volume, write down what enters and what leaves, and use conservation to find what you do not know — recycle, purge, yield, steam demand. Almost every later calculation is this same balance with more terms.
practice: Close a balance around a two-unit process with a recycle stream, and state your basis explicitly.
Calculate the cooling duty of a reactor from an energy balance, then sanity-check it against the measured temperature rise.
completionCriteria: You state your basis, units and assumption set before doing arithmetic.
Your balance closes to a tolerance you chose and defended, not to a rounding accident.

rows.name: Medical device regulation and quality systems
rows.summary: Risk management, design controls and the evidence trail that lets a device reach a patient.
rows.description: A device is not finished when it works — it is finished when there is traceable evidence that it works and that its risks are controlled. You learn the shape of a quality management system for medical devices, risk management in the ISO 14971 sense, the main approval routes and what post-market surveillance actually obliges you to do.
practice: Write a risk file outline for one simple device: intended use, hazards, controls, and the evidence for each control.
Take a published device and identify which classification route it would take in two different jurisdictions.
completionCriteria: You can distinguish a hazard, a hazardous situation and a risk, with an example of each.
You can state what a design change does to a risk file and which parts must be re-verified.

rows.name: Medical imaging basics
rows.summary: How X-ray, CT, MRI and ultrasound form an image, and what limits what you can see in it.
rows.description: Each modality trades off contrast, resolution, dose and time. You learn the physical interaction behind each one, the reconstruction idea that turns measurements into a picture, and the honest limits: artefacts, noise and the difference between a bright pixel and a diagnosis.
practice: Take one public image dataset and describe the artefacts you can see and what caused them.
Compare two modalities for one clinical question on contrast, dose and practicality.
completionCriteria: You can explain in one paragraph how an MRI signal is made to depend on tissue.
You can state the resolution, noise and artefact limits for a modality you are working with.

rows.name: Mobile app development
rows.summary: Cross-platform or native apps, navigation, offline behaviour and release builds.
rows.description: Mobile adds constraints: small screens, interrupted networks and platform packaging. Cross-platform tooling lets web skills go a long way.
practice: Build an app with two screens, local storage and a back-navigation flow.
Test the app offline and after an interrupted sync.
completionCriteria: The app behaves sensibly with no network.
You built an installable package and installed it on a device or emulator.

rows.name: Monitoring and observability
rows.summary: Metrics, logs, traces, alerting that respects sleep, and dashboards that answer questions.
rows.description: You cannot operate what you cannot see. Instrument first, then alert on symptoms rather than causes.
practice: Instrument a service with metrics and one useful dashboard.
Write an alert with a threshold and document its false-positive rate.
completionCriteria: Your dashboard answers three operational questions.
Every alert you create has a documented action.

rows.name: Network security and monitoring
rows.summary: Firewalls, TLS, logging, intrusion detection and triage.
rows.description: Detection needs data: logs, flows and alerts. Learn what normal looks like, then build simple detections and tune out noise.
practice: Set up a lab with a monitored host and generate benign plus suspicious traffic.
Write three detection rules and document false positives.
completionCriteria: You can triage an alert and justify a decision.
You can explain what your monitoring would miss.

rows.name: Operating systems and Linux
rows.summary: Processes, memory, files, permissions, the shell and scripting.
rows.description: Servers, containers and embedded devices are Linux. Comfort on the command line is a prerequisite for cloud, security and DevOps work.
practice: Complete a series of shell tasks: permissions, pipes, grep, process control.
Write a small shell script that automates a repetitive file task.
completionCriteria: You can navigate and manage a Linux system from the shell without a GUI.
You can explain file permissions and why they matter.

rows.name: Engineering physics: mechanics
rows.summary: Force, motion, energy and momentum applied to real machines and structures.
rows.description: The bridge between mathematics and physical design. Free-body diagrams and energy bookkeeping solve an enormous share of engineering problems before any software is involved.
practice: Draw free-body diagrams for a block on a slope and for an accelerating vehicle.
Predict the speed of a pendulum bob at the bottom of its swing, then verify with a stopwatch.
completionCriteria: You can draw a complete free-body diagram for a simple machine.
You can solve a work-energy problem without a formula sheet.

rows.name: Physiological modelling
rows.summary: Turning a body system into equations you can simulate, calibrate and doubt.
rows.description: Compartmental models, first-order kinetics and transport models make physiology computable. The craft is the same as any modelling: choose the structure for the question, state the parameters with their variation, and check the model against measurements it was not fitted to.
practice: Fit a two-compartment pharmacokinetic model to public data and report the residuals.
Change one parameter by 20 % and report how much the prediction moves.
completionCriteria: You can describe what your model deliberately leaves out and why that is acceptable for your question.
You can validate against data you did not fit on, or say clearly that you could not.

rows.name: Power electronics basics
rows.summary: Rectifiers, converters, switching and efficiency in power circuits.
rows.description: Power electronics link electronics to energy systems: converting and controlling large amounts of power efficiently — with real safety consequences.
practice: Simulate a buck converter and plot efficiency against load.
Explain why switching losses rise with frequency.
completionCriteria: You can describe the operating principle of a converter topology.
You can identify the safety-critical elements of a power design.

rows.name: Power systems and machines
rows.summary: Transformers, motors, generation, protection and grid basics.
rows.description: How electrical energy is generated, moved and used. Transformer and motor behaviour is the core, with safety and protection logic close behind.
practice: Compute transformer primary/secondary currents for a given load.
Interpret a motor datasheet and estimate torque at a given speed.
completionCriteria: You can explain a three-phase system and why it is used.
You can describe how a fault is detected and cleared.

rows.name: Probability and statistics
rows.summary: Describing uncertainty, sampling, distributions and testing claims with data.
rows.description: Statistics is what makes measurements trustworthy. You will use it to decide whether a sensor is biased, whether a model is better than a baseline, and whether a difference is real or noise.
practice: Compute mean and standard deviation of a real sensor log and interpret them.
Run a simple two-sample comparison on synthetic data and interpret the p-value honestly.
completionCriteria: You can explain why a small sample can mislead, with an example.
You can describe the difference between correlation and causation in your own words.

  n.tags = row.tags,
  n.verification = row.verification

rows.name: Process instrumentation and control
rows.summary: Sensors, control loops, tuning, and reading a P&ID as the working document it is.
rows.description: A process is only as good as the loop holding it steady. You learn what instruments measure and what they actually report, how transmitters, controllers, control valves and interlocks combine into a loop, and how to tune one without destabilising the unit next door.
practice: Trace one control loop on a real P&ID from sensor to final element and write your own loop description.
Tune a simulated flow or level loop and record how the response changes with each gain change.
completionCriteria: You can read a P&ID and say what each instrument tag is for.
You can explain the difference between a control loop and a safety interlock, with an example of each.

rows.name: Process safety and hazard analysis
rows.summary: Finding the ways a process can injure people or destroy equipment, before it does.
rows.description: Safety is a design activity, not a paragraph at the end of a report. You learn hazard identification, deviation-based studies such as HAZOP, layer-of-protection thinking, relief and flare basics, and how real incidents trace back to design and management decisions rather than one bad component.
practice: Run a small hazard study on a published flowsheet and record deviations, causes, consequences and safeguards.
Read one investigation report from a public safety board and list the design changes it recommended.
completionCriteria: You can distinguish a hazard from a risk, and a safeguard from an administrative control.
You can name the inherently safer option you would choose before adding another instrument.

rows.name: Steady-state process simulation
rows.summary: Building a flowsheet in a simulator, making it converge, and knowing when not to trust it.
rows.description: A simulator closes balances that would take days by hand, and it will supply a confident answer to a badly posed question. The skill is problem definition: property package, specification set, degrees of freedom, convergence, and reconciling the output against reality.
practice: Build and converge a two-column flowsheet, then reconcile its outlet stream against a hand balance.
Break your own simulation deliberately — remove a specification or choose the wrong property package — and describe the failure mode.
completionCriteria: You can count the degrees of freedom and say what each specification means physically.
You can list which results you verified independently and which you accepted from the simulator.

rows.name: Process thermodynamics and phase equilibria
rows.summary: How phases split, what a separation really costs, and where the thermodynamic limit sits.
rows.description: Property data and phase behaviour decide whether a separation is feasible and what it costs to run. You work with vapour-liquid equilibrium, activity models, equations of state and enthalpy departures, and you learn to distrust a property estimate that arrives without a source.
practice: Flash a binary mixture by hand and with a property library, then explain any disagreement between them.
Estimate the minimum energy of a separation from thermodynamics and compare it with a real design.
completionCriteria: You can say which model you used for a non-ideal mixture, and why that model.
You can state the thermodynamic limit of a proposed separation and how far the design is from it.

rows.name: Production planning and scheduling
rows.summary: Turning demand into a feasible plan: capacity, sequencing, queues and the cost of changeovers.
rows.description: A plan that ignores capacity is a wish. You work with demand and forecasting, aggregate capacity, bottleneck scheduling and setup trade-offs, and you learn the queueing intuition that tells you why utilisation above about eighty per cent makes lead times explode.
practice: Sequence a small order book through a two-machine shop and compare makespan across two rules.
Show how lead time responds as utilisation rises, using a simple queueing model.
completionCriteria: You can explain why a schedule that maximises machine utilisation can make delivery worse.
You can state your planning assumptions and what breaks them.

rows.name: Programming fundamentals
rows.summary: Variables, control flow, functions, files and basic debugging in one language.
rows.description: The first skill everything else in software depends on. Pick one language and get to the point where you can write a 100-line program without copying a tutorial.
practice: Write a program that reads a CSV, computes a summary and writes the result out.
Break a working program deliberately and fix it using the debugger rather than print statements.
completionCriteria: You can write a small program from an empty file without a tutorial.
You can read a traceback or stack trace and locate the fault.

rows.name: Solar PV system design
rows.summary: Panels, inverters, strings, shading, mounting and safety.
rows.description: Practical PV design: string sizing against inverter limits, shading analysis, earthing and protection — all with electrical safety rules that exist for good reasons.
practice: Design a string layout for a roof with known dimensions and one shaded area.
Produce a single-line diagram with protection devices labelled.
completionCriteria: Your design respects inverter voltage and current limits.
You documented isolation points and the safety rules that apply.

rows.name: Python programming
rows.summary: Idiomatic Python for scripting, data work and automation.
rows.description: Python is the working language of data, automation and much of engineering computation. Learn modules, virtual environments and error handling early.
practice: Build a command-line tool with argparse that processes a file and handles bad input.
Package a script into a module with a test file.
completionCriteria: You can structure a multi-file Python project and run it from the command line.
You handle errors explicitly instead of letting the program crash silently.

rows.name: Quality engineering and statistical process control
rows.summary: Control charts, capability and sampling: detecting when a process changed rather than when a part was bad.
rows.description: Inspection finds defects after the cost is spent; control charts find the change that causes them. You learn variable and attribute charts, the difference between control limits and specification limits, capability indices, and how to design a sampling plan that gives you a defensible answer.
practice: Build a control chart from a real measurement series and identify every out-of-control signal.
Calculate capability for a process and state whether the specification is realistic for it.
completionCriteria: You can explain why a point inside the specification limits can still be a signal.
You can say which chart suits an attribute measurement and why the others do not.

rows.name: Reaction engineering
rows.summary: Kinetics, reactor types and the operating point that sets conversion, selectivity and safety.
rows.description: Reactions rarely give you exactly what you want. You work with rate laws, residence time, CSTR and plug-flow behaviour, heat release and hot spots, and the difference between what a flask does and what a continuous reactor does at scale.
practice: Fit a rate law to published conversion data and state the confidence you have in the fit.
Size a CSTR and a plug-flow reactor for the same duty and explain why the volumes differ.
completionCriteria: You can explain why a hot spot forms and how you would remove that heat.
You state the assumptions behind your kinetics model rather than presenting the fit as truth.

rows.name: Remote sensing and imagery
rows.summary: Reading the planet from above: bands, resolution, reflectance, indices and the limits of what an image can tell you.
rows.description: Satellites measure reflected and emitted radiation, not photographs of the world. You learn the electromagnetic spectrum and band design, spatial, spectral, radiometric and temporal resolution, atmospheric effects, cloud masking, index calculation such as NDVI, classification, and the validation of anything you claim to have detected.
practice: Compute a vegetation or water index for two dates and explain the change you see.
Classify a small area and check part of the result against something you know on the ground.
completionCriteria: You can state the ground size of your smallest pixel and the smallest object you can honestly detect.
You can explain why a change in reflectance is not automatically a change on the ground.

rows.name: Renewable energy systems
rows.summary: Solar, wind and storage fundamentals; sizing and performance modelling.
rows.description: System-level renewable engineering: resource assessment, component sizing, conversion losses and honest payback estimates.
practice: Size a standalone PV-plus-battery system for a stated daily load with 2 days of autonomy.
Model monthly generation from irradiance data and compare with measured output.
completionCriteria: You can produce a sizing calculation with stated assumptions.
You state uncertainty and seasonal variation explicitly.

rows.name: Responsible AI practices
rows.summary: Bias, privacy, documentation, evaluation limits and human oversight.
rows.description: Models affect people. Documenting data provenance, known failure modes and limits is part of the engineering, and increasingly part of the law.
practice: Write a model card for a model you trained, including limitations and intended use.
Identify one bias risk in a public dataset and propose a mitigation.
completionCriteria: Your project documents what it must not be used for.
You can explain a privacy risk in a data pipeline you built.

rows.name: Robot kinematics
rows.summary: Coordinate frames, forward and inverse kinematics for arms and mobile robots.
rows.description: Kinematics answers “where will the tool be, and what joint angles get it there?” Matrix algebra is the working tool.
practice: Derive forward kinematics for a two-link planar arm.
Solve inverse kinematics for a target point and check reachability.
completionCriteria: You can derive and explain a transformation between frames.
You can identify a kinematic singularity.

rows.name: ROS 2 and robot software
rows.summary: Nodes, topics, services, transforms, simulation and launch files.
rows.description: ROS 2 is the standard robotics middleware: it gives you messaging, tooling and simulation so you can focus on behaviour.
practice: Build a two-node system publishing and subscribing to sensor data.
Simulate a differential-drive robot in Gazebo and command it to a target.
completionCriteria: Your system runs from a single launch file.
You can explain your node graph and message flow.

rows.name: Secure coding practices
rows.summary: Input validation, output encoding, parameterised queries, secrets and error handling.
rows.description: Most breaches start with a preventable coding mistake. This skill is about writing code that fails safely: validate input, encode output, never concatenate queries, never log secrets.
practice: Audit a small application for injection, XSS and secret leakage, and fix what you find.
Add rate limiting and request-size limits to an endpoint and test them.
completionCriteria: Your code uses parameterised queries everywhere.
Your error responses never leak stack traces or internal paths.

rows.name: Sensors and actuators
rows.summary: Interfacing sensors (I²C/SPI/analog), driving motors and accounting for real-world error.
rows.description: The physical interface is where projects succeed or fail: noise, calibration, power and mechanical alignment.
practice: Read a digital sensor over I²C and log calibrated values.
Drive a DC motor with a driver IC and measure speed versus duty cycle.
completionCriteria: You can calibrate a sensor against a reference and state the residual error.
You can explain your actuator’s power and current limits.

rows.name: Signals and systems basics
rows.summary: Sampling, frequency domain thinking, filters and aliasing.
rows.description: Any time you sample a sensor you are doing signal processing. Understanding sampling rate, aliasing and simple filters prevents a class of bugs that look like hardware faults.
practice: Sample a signal at two rates and demonstrate aliasing.
Design a simple moving-average or RC filter and measure its effect.
completionCriteria: You can choose a sampling rate for a given signal and justify it.
You can explain a filter’s effect in both time and frequency terms.

rows.name: Software design and architecture
rows.summary: Modules, interfaces, coupling, common patterns and refactoring safely.
rows.description: Design is about making change cheap. Learn to separate concerns, define interfaces, and refactor in small steps covered by tests.
practice: Refactor a long function into named units with tests, without changing behaviour.
Sketch the module boundaries for a small application before writing code.
completionCriteria: You can explain the responsibility of each module in your project.
You can change one module’s implementation without breaking others.

rows.name: Statistical modelling and inference
rows.summary: Regression, confidence intervals, experiment design and honest uncertainty.
rows.description: Modelling is asking whether an effect is real. Learn regression basics and, more importantly, how to report uncertainty instead of a single number.
practice: Fit a simple linear model and state the confidence interval for the slope.
Design an A/B test plan including sample size reasoning and stopping rules.
completionCriteria: You always report uncertainty alongside estimates.
You can explain what your model does not capture.

rows.name: Strength of materials
rows.summary: Stress, strain, deflection and failure in real components.
rows.description: Where statics stops, strength of materials continues: how much a beam bends, where a shaft will yield, and why sharp corners break things.
practice: Calculate the maximum bending stress in a loaded beam and compare with the material yield strength.
Design a bolt to carry a given shear load with a safety factor of two.
completionCriteria: You can compute a safety factor and explain what it protects against.
You can identify a stress concentration and propose a design fix.

rows.name: Structural analysis
rows.summary: Beams, frames and trusses: determinacy, deflections and load paths.
rows.description: Structural analysis decides member sizes and connection demands. Start with determinate structures, then understand how software handles the indeterminate ones.
practice: Check the determinacy of a frame and identify an unstable configuration.
Compare a hand calculation with a structural analysis tool for the same beam.
completionCriteria: You can explain the load path through a small building frame.
You can state when hand calculations are no longer sufficient.

rows.name: Supply chain and inventory management
rows.summary: Lead times, safety stock and the bullwhip effect: why the order you place is bigger than the demand you saw.
rows.description: Inventory exists because supply and demand do not arrive together. You learn lot sizing, reorder points and safety stock under uncertain demand, the amplification that runs up a supply chain, and how supplier quality and lead-time variability dominate almost everything else you do.
practice: Set a reorder point and safety stock for one item from its demand and lead-time variability.
Simulate the bullwhip effect in a four-tier chain and explain the amplification you see.
completionCriteria: You can explain why reducing lead-time variability can cut inventory more than cutting the average lead time.
You can state the service level your stock policy implies and what it costs.

rows.name: Terrain and surface modelling
rows.summary: Elevation data as a product: DEMs, slope, flow direction, contours and the error the surface carries.
rows.description: A digital elevation model answers questions about drainage, sight lines and cut and fill — at a stated resolution, with a stated vertical accuracy, and it is not the bare earth unless someone made it so. You work with surface and terrain models, slope and aspect, flow accumulation, contouring, profile extraction and vertical error.
practice: Derive slope and a flow-accumulation raster from an open DEM and identify the drainage lines.
Extract a profile between two points and compare it with a known elevation at one of them.
completionCriteria: You can explain the difference between a surface model and a bare-earth model with an example of where it changes the answer.
You can state the vertical accuracy of your data and what it prohibits you from concluding.

rows.name: Testing and debugging
rows.summary: Unit tests, edge cases, debuggers, logging and reproducing a bug.
rows.description: Testing is how you know the code works tomorrow. Debugging is a method, not luck: reproduce, isolate, hypothesise, test.
practice: Write unit tests for a function including two edge cases it currently fails.
Reproduce a reported bug from a written reproduction, then fix it and add a regression test.
completionCriteria: You can write a failing test before fixing a bug.
You can describe a bug in terms someone else can reproduce.

rows.name: Thermodynamics and heat transfer
rows.summary: Energy balances, efficiency limits and the three modes of heat transfer.
rows.description: Efficiency, cooling and energy cost are thermodynamic questions. You will use control-volume energy balances constantly in renewable and mechanical work.
practice: Compute the thermal efficiency of a simple cycle given input and output energy.
Estimate heat loss through a wall with conduction and convection in series.
completionCriteria: You can write an energy balance for a real device and identify losses.
You can explain why efficiency has a theoretical ceiling.

rows.name: Version control with Git
rows.summary: Commits, branches, merges, pull requests and recovery from mistakes.
rows.description: Every professional codebase uses version control. The essential skills are branching, reviewing a diff, resolving a conflict and getting out of trouble without deleting work.
practice: Create a branch, make two commits, open a pull request and merge it.
Create a deliberate merge conflict, resolve it, and explain each side.
completionCriteria: You can work on a branch and merge it cleanly.
You can undo a bad commit without losing unrelated work.

rows.name: Web frontend development
rows.summary: HTML, CSS, JavaScript/TypeScript, accessibility and responsive layout.
rows.description: Frontend is user experience plus engineering. Accessibility and performance are part of correctness, not extras.
practice: Build a responsive page and verify it with a keyboard only, no mouse.
Run an automated accessibility check and fix every serious finding.
completionCriteria: Your page works with keyboard only and at 320 px width.
You can explain how you handled loading and error states.

rows.name: Work design, ergonomics and human factors
rows.summary: Designing the task around a person who is tired, interrupted and built like an actual body.
rows.description: The cheapest improvement is often a change in how the work is arranged. You learn work measurement and standard time, task analysis, lifting and posture risk, attention and error, and how to change a workstation so the work is both faster and less damaging to the person doing it.
practice: Analyse one repetitive task for posture and force risk and propose two changes that remove the risk rather than the symptom.
Time-study a task and state the allowances and rating assumptions behind your standard time.
completionCriteria: You can distinguish a human error from a system that made the error likely.
You can justify a workstation change on both output and injury-risk grounds.
